**A type named exactly `Exception` is left alone.** It is either `System.Exception` itself, seen while analysing a framework, or a deliberate shadow whose author already knows; "derive from `Exception`" is not advice that means anything to a type named `Exception`.

**An unresolved base is silence, not a finding.** If any type in the base chain is an error type the rule stops and says nothing, because "does not derive from `Exception`" and "the compilation could not tell" produce the same answer from a naive walk and only one of them is a finding. This is why the rule is semantic and does not run under `--load=loose`.

⚠ **No fix, deliberately.** The two repairs are adding `: Exception` — which changes what the type *is*, and drags in the constructors and the serialization surface an exception is expected to have — and renaming, which is a solution-wide edit that Skala's one-file text-edit model cannot make. Guessing between them would be guessing at intent. `hasFix: false` is the first in the catalogue and is a knowing choice rather than an omission.

**The shape that is genuinely borderline** is a name ending in the word by accident: `ThrowsNoException`, `AssertsOnException`. They are rare, they read badly to a human as well, and they are the case to baseline.

rules.title: A type name repeats the keyword the declaration already carries
rules.summary: `class OrderClass` and `struct PointStruct` say the same thing twice; the keyword is already there, two words to the left.
rules.rationale: A type's kind is written in its declaration, and every tool that shows the type shows the keyword: the IDE's completion list, the hover, the go-to-definition, the diff. Repeating it in the identifier spends a word on information the reader already has, and it costs the name whatever a real noun would have contributed — `OrderClass` is a worse name than `Order`, not a more precise one. The suffix is also the first thing to go stale, because it survives the edit that makes it wrong: a `class` that becomes a `record` keeps its `Class` suffix until somebody notices. This is not `CA1711`, which is about suffixes .NET has *reserved* — `Attribute`, `Collection`, `EventArgs`. These are not reserved; they are simply empty.
rules.falsePositives:
**Only two suffixes, and the declaration has to agree with the one it uses.** `Class` is reported on a `class` or a `record` (a record class is a class, and a `record OrderClass` is the stale suffix in its most literal form); `Struct` is reported on a `struct` or a `record struct`. Where the name and the keyword *disagree* — a `class` called `PointStruct` — the rule says nothing, because there the name is not redundant, it is wrong, and "delete the suffix" is the wrong advice for a name that lies about its kind.

⚠ **`Record` is deliberately not a suffix this rule knows about, even though the proposal names it.** `Record` was a domain noun for a row of data for decades before it was a C# keyword: `LogRecord`, `AuditRecord`, `MedicalRecord`, `DnsRecord`, `ResourceRecord`, `ActivationRecord`, `ChangeRecord`. There is no syntactic test that separates the noun from the redundant suffix, the noun is overwhelmingly the more common of the two, and a rule that cannot tell them apart on a word this common would be wrong far more often than right. `PersonRecord` goes unreported. That is the price of not reporting `LogRecord`, and it is worth paying.

**A curated list of compound words is exempt, and it is judgement rather than measurement.** The rule reads the PascalCase word immediately before the suffix, and stays silent when it is one of: `Base`, `Sub`, `Super`, `Inner`, `Outer`, `Nested`, `Abstract`, `Sealed`, `Partial`, `Generic`, `Derived`, `Test`, `Master`, `Character`, `Equivalence`, `Storage`, `Business`, `Economy`, `First`, `Second`, `Weight`, `Size`, `Device`, `Object`, `Working`, `Worker`, `Ref`, `Readonly`. Two different things are on that list. In `MasterClass`, `CharacterClass`, `EquivalenceClass`, `StorageClass`, `BusinessClass` and `WeightClass` the word "class" means *category* and is not about C# at all. In `BaseClass`, `InnerClass`, `NestedClass`, `AbstractClass` and `TestClass` the type is *about* a class — a fixture, a sample, a node in a tool that reads C# — so the word is the head noun rather than a suffix; `TestClass` in particular is MSTest's own attribute name and a term of art. ⚠ **The list is incomplete by construction and always will be.** English compounds are not enumerable, and a name whose last word is a real compound and is not on this list will be reported wrongly. Add a `#pragma` or a baseline entry; the rule ships at `suggestion` because that is the honest severity for a judgement of this kind.

**Two mechanical guards keep the obvious noise out.** The name must be longer than the suffix, so a `class Class` or a `struct Struct` in a parser or a code generator — where that is the whole subject — is never reported. And the character before the suffix must be lower-case or a digit, so the suffix has to begin a new PascalCase word after a real one; an all-caps run running into it is not a suffix boundary anyone wrote on purpose.

⚠ **No fix.** Renaming a type rewrites every reference to it across a solution, and Skala's fix model is a list of text edits against one file's `SourceText` — an edit that renamed the declaration and nothing else would produce a tree that does not build. Choosing the replacement name is a person's decision in any case; `Order` is usually right and is not always right.

rules.title: A type has no members, no base and no attributes
rules.summary: A `class Foo { }` that derives from nothing, carries no attribute and declares nothing is a declaration that was started and not finished.
rules.rationale: An empty type is usually one of four things, and three of them are legitimate patterns: a marker attribute, a marker interface, a named specialisation of a generic base, or the leftovers of an edit. Only the fourth is a finding, and the first three are all recognisable from the declaration itself — an attribute has a base or an attribute list, a marker interface is an interface, and a specialisation has a base list. What is left is a type with nothing attached to it in any direction: no members, no base, no interfaces, no attributes, no type parameters, not `partial`. That is not a marker, because nothing can key on it; it is a name and a pair of braces. Either it is about to become something and the declaration landed early, or it stopped being something and the members were deleted around it.

examples.bad: public sealed class OrderProcessor { }
examples.good:
[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class)]
public sealed class AuditedAttribute : Attribute { }

rules.falsePositives:
**The exemptions are the rule.** A detector for "no members" is three lines; deciding which empty types are deliberate is the whole of this one, and each answer is decidable from the declaration alone.

**A marker interface is a real pattern and is never reported.** `interface IAggregateRoot { }` is how a codebase tags types for a generic constraint, for assembly scanning, or for a dispatcher — and an interface is the *only* correct shape for that, because it is the only one a type can adopt without changing what it inherits from. Every empty interface is out of scope, no further test.

**A marker attribute is never reported either**, and it does not need to be recognised as one: any declaration carrying an attribute list, or any declaration with a base list, is exempt — and every attribute type has at least one of the two. That also covers `[JsonSerializable]`-style declarations whose whole purpose is to be read by a generator, and `[ApiController]`-style types whose behaviour is entirely in a framework.

**A base list is an exemption on its own.** `class StringList : List<string> { }` names a closed generic, `class SqlOrderRepository : RepositoryBase<Order> { }` is a leaf of a closed hierarchy, and `class TimeoutFailure : Failure { }` is a case in a sealed-hierarchy discriminated union — three shapes where the declaration carries all its meaning in the base list and the empty body is correct. ⚠ This also puts an empty exception type, which the proposal wanted reported, out of scope. `class NotFoundException : Exception { }` is a real complaint — the type cannot carry a message — but it is `CA1032`'s complaint, it is stated better there, and separating "an exception with no constructors" from "a leaf of a closed hierarchy" needs semantics this rule does not have.

**`partial` is never reported.** The other part may be in another file, or may not exist yet because a generator writes it. This single exemption is what keeps the rule out of every source-generated codebase.

**A generic empty type is never reported.** `class Metres { }` used as `Quantity<Metres>` is a phantom type, and `class Marker<T> { }` is the generic version of one; a type parameter is a strong signal that the type exists to be *named* rather than instantiated.

**A bodyless `record Foo;` is never reported.** The semicolon form exists precisely to declare a complete type with nothing in it — a unit or a message in a message-based codebase — so writing one is a statement rather than an omission. `record Foo { }`, with braces around nothing, is reported.

⚠ **The shape that remains genuinely ambiguous is the non-generic phantom type**: `sealed class Metres { }` with no base and no attribute, used only as a type argument. It is reported, and it is a false positive. Deciding otherwise would need to know every use of the type, which is a whole-compilation question and this rule is syntactic by design. Suppress it or baseline it; the rule ships at `suggestion` for this reason.

⚠ **No fix.** Deleting a type is not a mechanical edit — something may name it, including code the compilation cannot see, such as reflection, a DI registration by name, or a serialised payload. Filling it in is not mechanical either. The finding says look at this; it does not say what to do.

rules.title: Use `T?` instead of `Nullable<T>`
rules.summary: A bound `System.Nullable<T>` is written in long form where `T?` names exactly the same type.
rules.rationale: `T?` is the spelling every other nullable in the file already uses, so the long form reads as though it meant something different. It is also the form older samples and generated code produce, which is why an assistant writes it: the training data is full of `Nullable<int>` and the language stopped needing it in C# 2.

examples.bad: Nullable<int> total = null;
examples.good: int? total = null;

rules.falsePositives: The name is bound before anything is reported, so a user-defined `Nullable<T>` is never touched. Positions where the short form is not legal syntax are excluded rather than rewritten: the unbound `typeof(Nullable<>)`, a `cref` or `nameof` argument, a `using` alias, a member-access receiver, a pointer element type, and any pattern or `is` type test, because C# rejects a nullable value type in a pattern. Comments and preprocessor directives inside the type name are excluded because the rewrite deletes the text they live in.

rules.title: Use a compound assignment
rules.summary: An assignment whose right-hand side is a binary operation on the assignment target itself, where the compound operator says it once.
rules.rationale: Naming the target twice is the shape a rename can half-finish: `total = subtotal + 1` compiles and is a different program, and nothing in the long form says which of the two occurrences was meant. The compound form cannot drift, and it is the form C# has had since version 1 — the long one is what a model writes because most of its training data predates the habit.

examples.bad: count = count + 1;
examples.good: count += 1;

rules.falsePositives: The direction is safe and the reverse is not: C# defines `x op= y` as `x = (T)(x op y)` with an explicit conversion back to the target's type, which the long form lacks — `byte b; b = b + 1;` does not compile at all, so the rule never sees the shapes where the conversion differs. A cast on the right-hand side is therefore never unwrapped: `long l; l = (int)(l + 1);` truncates and `l += 1` does not. Only whole expression statements are reported, the target must be a chain of plain names so that the two forms evaluate it the same number of times, and the binary operator's left operand must be that same target textually — which excludes `x = x + a + b`, whose left operand is `x + a`. `&&` and `||` have no compound spelling and are excluded. Comments and preprocessor directives between the target and the operator are excluded because the fix deletes that text.
rules.resharperNote: The export sets `resharper_convert_to_compound_assignment_highlighting = hint` while this rule defaults to `suggestion`. Reading the ReSharper key with `--resharper-severities` therefore lowers it: ReSharper treats the long form as a cosmetic preference, and Skala treats it as the shape a half-finished rename hides in.

rules.title: The nested `if` statements can be combined
rules.summary: An `if` whose entire body is another `if` with no `else` is one condition written as two.
rules.rationale: The second `if` adds a level of nesting and no branch: there is no path where the outer condition holds and the inner one does not lead anywhere else. `&&` short-circuits, so the merged form evaluates exactly what the nested one did, in the same order — and it stops the nesting counting against the `SK7006` depth metric for a structure that never had two branches.
rules.falsePositives: A whole chain is one finding reported at its top, so the fix never overlaps another and the rule is silent after its own fix. Any `else` anywhere in the chain excludes it, as does an outer body holding anything besides the inner `if`. An operand that `&&` would capture — `||`, `??`, a conditional or an assignment — is parenthesised rather than merged flat. Names a merged condition introduces (a pattern variable, an `out var`) have their scope widened by the rewrite, so the whole member is scanned for a colliding declaration first and the finding is dropped if one exists; the scan deliberately over-bails, counting names that could never conflict. Comments and preprocessor directives anywhere outside the surviving body exclude the chain, and so does a `#` inside a condition's string literal.

rules.title: The `for` loop is a `while`
rules.summary: A `for` with no initializer and no incrementor is a `while` written with two empty clauses.
rules.rationale: `for` promises a bound and then declares none, so a reader has to check both semicolons to find out there is nothing in them. The rewrite is exact rather than merely equivalent: with no incrementors, `continue` jumps to the condition in both forms, and nothing else in a `for` is being used.
rules.falsePositives: `for (;;)` is deliberately not reported: it is the idiomatic infinite loop, and `while (true)` says nothing the original did not. A declaration, an initializer or an incrementor in any clause excludes the loop — converting a `for (int i = 0; c;)` would have to lift the declaration into the enclosing scope, which is a different rewrite with a different risk. Comments and preprocessor directives inside the empty clauses exclude it too, because the fix replaces the whole header.

rules.title: Use `string.IsNullOrEmpty`
rules.summary: A null test on a string followed by an emptiness test on the same string, or the negation of both.
rules.rationale: The hand-written form states the check twice and gets its order wrong easily — `x.Length == 0 || x == null` dereferences null before it tests for it. `string.IsNullOrEmpty` also carries `[NotNullWhen(false)]`, so the compiler's null analysis learns from the call what it cannot learn from the pair.
rules.falsePositives: `x.Length == 0` and `x == ""` are both reported and are the same check: string `==` is ordinal value equality that compares lengths first. `string.Empty` counts as the literal. ⚠ The rule this one must not become is `IsNullOrWhiteSpace`: `x == null || x.Trim().Length == 0` is a different predicate — true for a single space, where `IsNullOrEmpty` is false — and nothing separates the two shapes except what stands between the receiver and `.Length`. Two guards therefore do two different jobs: the emptiness test must be on the same expression the null test named, which is what excludes `Trim()`, and that expression must be a chain of plain names, which is what excludes the double evaluation a call or an indexer would suffer. The receiver must also bind to `System.String`, so an array's `Length` is never matched, and the null test must come first. A longer `||` chain is only matched where the pair is a single subexpression, which left-associativity makes true for `x == null || x.Length == 0 || y` and false for `y || x == null || x.Length == 0`. Comments and preprocessor directives inside the expression exclude it.

rules.title: A variable already owned by `using` is disposed again
rules.summary: `Dispose()` is called by hand on a variable whose `using` disposes it at the end of the scope anyway.
rules.rationale: A `using` disposes its resource when the scope ends, on every path including the exceptional one, so an explicit `Dispose()` on the same variable is a second call that the language guarantees will happen. Double disposal is only harmless for a type whose `Dispose` is idempotent — the framework asks for that and not every type delivers it, and a second call that releases a handle number the process has since reissued corrupts an unrelated file rather than throwing. Deleting the call removes the second disposal without changing when the first one happens.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The fix is safe because of a language guarantee rather than an analysis.** A `using` variable is read-only, so nothing between the declaration and the explicit call can have made the two disposals land on different objects; the rule does not have to prove it. ⚠ Ownership is read from the variable's own declarator, never from an enclosing `using` that happens to name the same identifier — a shadowing local of the same name in an inner scope is a different symbol and is not reported. ⚠ The call must be an entire statement directly inside a block: `if (failed) reader.Dispose();` is the same redundancy and is not reported, because deleting the statement would leave an `if` with no body, and a fix that produces text which does not parse is the one failure a fixing tool may not have. A `Dispose()` whose result is read, or one behind an `&&`, has nothing the fix can remove. ⚠ The invoked member is resolved by the semantic model and must be the parameterless disposal contract the `using` will itself invoke — `Dispose` is an ordinary identifier and a type may declare one that does something else. `Close()` is not reported: it is a different method, it is not always an alias for `Dispose`, and deleting it is not the same edit. A call reached across a lambda or a local function is skipped, because when that body runs is not something the enclosing `using` says anything about.

rules.title: The `using` resource is built with an object initializer
rules.summary: `using var x = new Foo { Bar = Baz() };` — the object initializer runs before the `using` owns anything, so an initializer that throws leaks the constructed resource.
rules.rationale: The `using` protects what is assigned to its variable, and an object initializer runs after the constructor and before that assignment. So `using var x = new Foo { Bar = Baz() }` has a window in which a fully constructed `Foo` — with its handle, its socket, its pooled buffer — exists and nothing owns it: if `Baz()` throws, the object is unreachable, no `Dispose` ever reaches it, and the code reads as if the `using` covered it. The leak is invisible in every test where the initializer does not throw, which is all of them. Constructing first and assigning afterwards moves the assignment inside the scope the `using` protects, and it is a mechanical edit.

examples.bad:
using var writer = new StreamWriter(path) { AutoFlush = Configured() };
writer.WriteLine("done");

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The rule reports only the shapes the hoist has somewhere to land.** `using (Open() { … })` declares no name to assign through, and a `using` statement whose body is not a block has no place to put the assignments; both are the same bug and neither is reported, because a finding a fix cannot honour is worse than a missing one. The declaration must have a single declarator whose initializer is literally a `new` with an object initializer. ⚠ **Reference types only.** A `using` local is read-only, so `x.Member = value` on a struct-typed one is CS1654 — the hoisted form does not compile and there is no other one. ⚠ **A `required` member makes the hoist illegal rather than awkward**: the object initializer is what satisfies the requirement, so `new Foo()` alone is CS9035 and the type is skipped entirely. ⚠ Every initializer member must be a plain `Name = value` whose target is a settable property or a writable field: an `init` accessor is assignable in an object initializer and nowhere else, and a nested initializer (`A = { B = 1 }`), an indexed one (`[0] = v`) and a collection element are different rewrites that this rule does not attempt. Accessibility needs no check — the hoisted assignment sits where the initializer did and obeys the same rules. ⚠ **A comment inside the initializer withdraws the finding.** The hoist rebuilds the assignments from their expressions, and trivia between two members belongs to no expression, so it would go out with the braces — silently, under a fix marked safe. The reference tree has exactly this: an `IrradianceFieldRenderer` initializer carrying a six-line note about which pass reads the bound names. ⚠ **A constant initializer is reported too.** `new Foo { Retries = 3 }` cannot throw and therefore cannot leak, and the finding on it is about the shape rather than a proven leak; separating the two would mean deciding which expressions can throw, which is not decidable and is exactly the guessing that turns a rule into a nuisance in the other direction.

rules.title: A variable captured by `using` is returned
rules.summary: `return x;` where `x` is owned by an enclosing `using`, so the caller receives an object that was disposed on the way out.
rules.rationale: A `using` disposes at the `return`, before the value reaches the caller, so the method's signature and its body disagree: it says "here is a resource" and delivers one that is already closed. The caller gets an `ObjectDisposedException` on first use, from a method that reads as correct — or, for a type whose `Dispose` only returns a pooled buffer, no exception at all and silent corruption once that buffer is handed to somebody else.

examples.good: Stream Open(string path) => File.OpenRead(path);

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **No fix, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** Deleting the `using` makes the method leak; keeping it makes the method wrong. Which the author meant is the whole question and no edit answers it, so the finding is a report. ⚠ **The `Task` shape belongs to `SK3007`.** The two rules overlap on exactly one shape — `return x;` where `x` is a `using` variable of a task type — and `SK3007` is the one carrying a fix for it, so this rule tests the type and stays quiet rather than being deduplicated after the fact. `supersedes` was considered and rejected: it dedupes on a shared span and would have suppressed the finding that has the fix. Where `SK3007` declines the shape because it cannot rewrite the whole method, neither rule reports, which is a known gap. ⚠ **The returned expression must be the variable itself.** `return x.Stream;` and `return Wrap(x);` hand out something whose lifetime may well depend on `x`, and proving that needs to know what the member or the method did with it; guessing about ownership is how a rule comes to report the correct code around the incorrect code. ⚠ The `return` and the `using` must belong to the same member, lambda or local function: a `return` inside a lambda returns from the lambda, and a lambda closing over a `using` variable may run at a time the `using` says nothing about.

rules.title: The non-`async` `Task` method returns null
rules.summary: A method whose declared return type is `Task` or `Task<T>` and which is not `async` returns `null` or `default`.
rules.rationale: A `Task` return type invites the caller to write `await Something()`, and awaiting null is a `NullReferenceException` whose stack names the caller rather than the method that produced it. An `async` method cannot do this — the compiler wraps whatever it returns — so the shape exists only where the signature was written by hand, and there `return null;` looks exactly like every other "nothing to do" in the file. `Task.CompletedTask` is the completed task the caller was promised.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The fix is unsafe by declaration and the generic form is why.** `Task.CompletedTask` is the only completed non-generic task there is, so that half is mechanical; `Task.FromResult<T>(default!)` picks a *value* the method never named, and what a completed task should carry is a decision about the method rather than an edit. Applying it turns a crash into a default result, which is the point of the rule and is still a behaviour change somebody should read. ⚠ Only ordinary methods and local functions, only where the declared return type resolves to `System.Threading.Tasks.Task` or `Task<T>`, and only for a literal `null` or `default` — a null-valued local, a conditional whose branch is null, and a `default(Task)` are the same bug and are not matched, because the rule reports what it can rewrite in one span. ⚠ **`async` withdraws it**: `async Task<string>` returning `null` returns a null *string* inside a real task, which is an ordinary nullable-reference question. ⚠ **`Task?` withdraws it too**, because the author has declared that null is a value this method returns and the contract already carries the warning. `ValueTask` is not covered: it is a struct and cannot be null. ⚠ The replacement is not built by editing the declaration's text — an alias (`using MyTask = System.Threading.Tasks.Task;`) makes the written name resolve to something a string edit would get wrong. The rule asks whether the simple name `Task` means `System.Threading.Tasks.Task` at that position and falls back to the fully qualified name, which always binds.

rules.title: A `SpinLock` is stored in a `readonly` field
rules.summary: A field of type `System.Threading.SpinLock` is declared `readonly`, so every caller takes the lock on a defensive copy.
rules.rationale: `SpinLock` is a mutable struct and its state *is* the lock. `Enter` is not a `readonly` member, so reading a `readonly` field to call it makes the compiler take a defensive copy: the lock is acquired on a temporary and released on a temporary, and nothing is ever excluded. It compiles, it runs, `lockTaken` comes back true every time, and the race the lock was written to prevent is exactly as it was — with the code above it saying otherwise. Removing `readonly` is the only repair.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The fix is one word and it is not cosmetic.** Removing `readonly` makes the field assignable and makes every call site operate on the real lock instead of a copy, which changes what the program does — for the better, and still not without review. `fixIsSafe` is false for that reason rather than because the edit is uncertain: there is exactly one repair and no intent to guess at. ⚠ The type is resolved by the semantic model and never matched on the written name: `SpinLock` is a plausible name for somebody's own type and stripping `readonly` from a field of one would be a change made for no reason. ⚠ **One finding per declaration, not per declarator.** `readonly SpinLock a, b;` has one `readonly` token, and two findings would carry the same deletion twice. ⚠ **An instance field inside a `readonly struct` is the same bug and is withheld, because the fix would not compile.** CS8340 requires every instance field of a `readonly struct` to be `readonly`, so the keyword there is not the author's choice and deleting it is an error rather than a repair; the lock is just as broken, and the repair is to stop the containing type being a `readonly struct`, which is a design change and not an edit. The same applies to a `SpinLock` returned from a property or exposed through an `in` parameter.

rules.title: An `out` variable is declared and never read
rules.summary: `M(out var x)` where nothing ever mentions `x` again declares a name for a value the code has decided not to look at; `out _` says that.
rules.rationale: An `out` argument is a second return value, and a declaration expression is how the caller receives it. When the receiving name is never read, the declaration is doing one thing only — satisfying the signature — and it does that while adding a name to the enclosing scope, a definite-assignment obligation, and a line the next reader has to check before concluding it does not matter. `out _` is the language's word for exactly this: the argument is required, the value is not wanted. It also removes the name from scope, so a later edit cannot accidentally read a value nobody meant to keep, and it makes the two `TryGetValue` calls in a file that differ only in whether the value is used visibly different from each other.
rules.falsePositives:
**This is one of the nine inspections issue #121 grouped, and it is the only one shipped.** It is the shape with a mechanical, always-safe repair: the callee writes the argument either way, so replacing the declaration with a discard cannot remove a side effect. Removing an unread *ordinary* local cannot promise that — `var response = Send();` is unread and deleting it stops the request — and the remaining seven shapes each need something a single declaration does not carry. `UnusedLocalFunction` is already **CS8321**, a compiler warning, and is not re-implemented here. `NotAccessedVariable`, `UnusedLocalFunctionParameter`, `UnusedTypeParameter` and `UnusedParameterInPartialMethod` have no safe edit; `UnusedLocalFunctionReturnValue` and `UnusedTupleComponentInReturnValue` need every call site. What is left uncovered is named rather than implied, so [17](17-inspection-parity.md)'s residue keeps counting it.

**Only a declaration expression in an `out` argument position.** A pre-declared local (`int n; M(out n);`) is not reported: the declaration is a statement of its own, the repair is to delete it as well as the reference, and that is two edits in two places rather than one replacement. A discard already written is not a declaration and produces nothing.

**Never read *and* never written.** Any reference to the local at all withdraws the finding, including one that only assigns it and one that passes it to a second `out`. That is stricter than "never read" and it is deliberate: `out _` deletes the name, so a finding that only proves the value is unread would produce an edit that does not compile wherever the name is used for anything else.

**A second, redundant guard reads tokens rather than operations.** Before reporting, the enclosing operation blocks are scanned for any identifier token spelling the same name. A match withdraws the finding even when the operation tree showed no reference — the case it is there for is `nameof(x)`, and the cost of being wrong in this direction is one missed finding rather than one broken build. A member or a type with the same name as the variable also silences it; that is the price and it is small.

⚠ **A member containing a preprocessor directive is skipped entirely.** Disabled text is trivia, so a reference inside `#if DEBUG` is invisible to both the operation tree and the token scan, and under another configuration the variable is read. This is the same refusal `SK6003` and `SK6020` make for the same reason.

⚠ **A parameter whose type mentions one of the invoked method's own type parameters is skipped, conservatively.** `out _` is an implicitly typed discard, and CS8183 is what a discard that cannot be typed produces. Whether inference actually fails depends on the rest of the call, and answering that properly means re-running overload resolution; declining is cheaper and only ever costs findings. The related shape the rule cannot see at all is an overload set whose members differ *only* in the `out` parameter's type, where `out _` becomes ambiguous — vanishingly rare, and a compiler error rather than a silent change if it happens.

rules.title: A `foreach` variable is declared wider than the element it receives
rules.summary: `foreach (object item in names)` over a `List<string>` throws the element type away at the top of the loop and makes the body ask for it back.
rules.rationale: The collection already knows what it holds. Declaring the loop variable as a base type discards that at the one point in the method where it was free, and everything downstream pays: the body cannot call the element's own members without a cast or a pattern, the reader cannot tell what is in the collection without following the collection back to its declaration, and where the element is a value type every iteration boxes. Naming the element type is not extra precision — it is the precision the collection was carrying anyway, written down.
rules.falsePositives:
**Only a widening the compiler would have performed implicitly, and only two kinds of it.** The conversion from the element type to the declared type must be an implicit *reference* conversion or a *boxing* conversion — a base class, an implemented interface, or `object`. An identity conversion is nothing to report; an implicit *numeric* one (`foreach (long value in ints)`) is not a lost type but a deliberate arithmetic width, and narrowing it would change what the body computes; an implicit *nullable* one (`foreach (int? value in ints)`) is the author saying the loop deals in absence; a *user-defined* one is somebody's operator and not a widening at all. An **explicit** conversion — `foreach (string text in objects)`, which `foreach` uniquely permits — is a downcast the author wrote on purpose and is the opposite of this finding.

**`var` is never reported.** It already is the element type, and the whole rule is the request to write that type down.

**The iteration variable cannot be assigned**, so the shape that would make this dangerous does not exist: CS1656 forbids `item = …` inside the loop. That is why there is no dataflow guard here and no fixture for one.

**Three shapes are skipped because the fix could not be written.** An anonymous element type has no name to write; a `dynamic` element type is not a type this question applies to; and an element type the containing assembly cannot see (`Compilation.IsSymbolAccessibleWithin` answers it) would produce a name that does not bind. The suggested type is rendered with `ToMinimalDisplayString` against the position of the loop, so it uses the file's own `using` directives and never introduces one.

⚠ **The interface case is the one most likely to be deliberate.** `foreach (IShape shape in circles)` is reported, and "program to the interface" is a real reason to have written it. So is a base class chosen to say that the loop body only needs the base. The rule ships at `suggestion` for this reason: it is an observation about what the collection knows, not a claim about what the author meant.

⚠ **The fix is `fixIsSafe: false` and the reason is overload resolution.** `Write(item)` binding to `Write(string)` instead of `Write(object)` is a different program, and a `switch` arm inside the body may become CS8121 — a pattern the narrower type can no longer match. Both are visible on review and the second is a compiler error rather than a silent change, but neither is an edit to apply unread. Where the element type is nullable the narrowed declaration also inherits the annotation, which is correct and may surface a CS8602 the wider type was hiding.

rules.title: The lambda captures nothing and is not `static`
rules.summary: A lambda, anonymous method or local function that references nothing outside itself can be `static`, and then it cannot allocate a closure.
rules.rationale: A lambda that captures a local or `this` is compiled into a display class, and every evaluation of the lambda expression allocates one — or, where the compiler can cache it, keeps the captured object alive for the lifetime of the cache. A lambda that captures nothing has neither cost, and the compiler is free to cache one delegate instance for the whole program. `static` is the keyword that says so and the compiler that checks it: the modifier is a compile-time assertion that the body references no enclosing local, parameter, `this` or `base`, so a `static` lambda that compiles is a lambda that provably allocates no environment. That makes it the rare performance edit with no judgement in it — the fix is one keyword, the compiler verifies the claim, and a later edit that starts capturing is rejected at the point it is written instead of silently reintroducing the allocation.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ The rule reports only what it can prove, and every unproven shape is declined. The body is walked in full — including nested lambdas, local functions and query clauses — and any of the following withholds the finding: `this` or `base`; a local, parameter or range variable declared outside the reported declaration, which includes a primary constructor parameter and the implicit `value` of a setter; an instance field, property, event or method reached without a receiver; a call to a local function declared outside, whose own captures this rule cannot see; and any name the semantic model does not resolve, so a file with errors reports nothing rather than guessing. Names that cannot capture are admitted: types, namespaces, aliases, labels, discards, static members, and everything inside `nameof`. Lambdas converted to an expression tree rather than to a delegate are excluded, as is any lambda nested inside one. A declaration already marked `static` is not reported, and neither is anything below C# 9. ⚠ **Disjoint from `SK4002` by construction**: that rule reports a delegate capturing iteration-local storage, and a declaration this rule reports captures nothing at all, so no declaration can produce both. ⚠ The fix does not claim an allocation was measured — it claims the allocation is now impossible.
rules.resharperNote: The export sets `resharper_lambda_expression_can_be_made_static_highlighting = none`, so a repository that reads ReSharper's key gets this rule switched off. Skala ships it at `suggestion`: the inspection is quiet in the export because JetBrains treats it as a style opportunity, and the parity measurement makes it the highest-volume quiet inspection in the whole survey.

rules.title: The private method does not use instance state
rules.summary: A private instance method whose body never touches `this` can be `static`, which drops the hidden argument and the null check.
rules.rationale: An instance call passes a `this` argument the method does not read and, through a reference, carries a null check the callee cannot avoid. Making the method `static` removes both, and the declaration then states the fact the body already established: this code depends on its arguments and on nothing else. That is the larger half of the value — a reader no longer has to read the body to learn whether the method participates in the object's state, and a later edit that starts using a field is rejected at the point it is written. The rule is deliberately restricted to `private` methods, where the change is invisible outside the type; `static` on a visible member is an API change and a different decision.
rules.falsePositives: Only an ordinary `private` method with a body, in a non-partial class, struct or record declared once in one file, is considered. `static`, `abstract`, `virtual`, `override`, `partial`, `extern` and `new` declarations are excluded, as is anything carrying an attribute — a serialization callback, a marked event handler and a framework-invoked method are all shapes where the signature is a contract rather than a choice. The body is walked with the same proof `SK4020` uses, so any `this`, `base`, instance member or unresolved name withholds the finding; a recursive call to the method itself is admitted, because the fix makes that call static too. ⚠ Every call site in the file is then checked, and a single `this.Method()` or `instance.Method()` withholds the finding, because that spelling does not compile against a static method. ⚠ **What the rule cannot see is reflection**: a private method found by name through `MethodInfo` and invoked with an instance target breaks when it becomes static, and no analyzer can prove the absence of that. It also cannot see another file, which is why a partial containing type is excluded rather than analysed.

rules.title: The struct is never mutated and is not `readonly`
rules.summary: A struct with only readonly state and no member that assigns `this` can be `readonly`, which deletes the defensive copies.
rules.rationale: The compiler cannot know that a struct's members leave it alone, so wherever the struct is reached through storage it may not write — a `readonly` field, an `in` parameter, a `ref readonly` return, a `foreach` variable — it copies the whole value before every member call. `SK2005` and `SK4007` report two consequences of exactly that. The `readonly` modifier is the declaration that removes the doubt: the compiler verifies that no member writes to the instance and then stops emitting the copies. The keyword is not a hint or a tuning parameter; it is a fact about the type that the type already satisfied and had not written down.
rules.falsePositives: The proof is the compiler's own rule for `readonly struct`, checked before the keyword is proposed: every instance field must already be `readonly`, no instance property or indexer may have a `set` accessor, and no member may assign to `this`, pass it by `ref` or `out`, or increment it. `init` accessors are admitted, because a `readonly struct` permits them. Excluded outright: a struct already `readonly`, a `partial` or multiply-declared struct, a `ref struct`, a `record struct` — where the modifier would turn positional `set` accessors into `init` and change the public API — anything `unsafe` or holding a `fixed` buffer or a pointer, a field-like `event`, whose backing field cannot be readonly, and a struct that already spells `readonly` on one of its members. Nested types inside the struct are not searched, because `this` there is a different instance. ⚠ **The modifier is not a no-op for consumers even though it is source-compatible**: an `in` parameter and a `readonly` field stop copying, so a member that returned a value derived from a stale copy now returns the current one. That is the bug the copies were hiding rather than a behaviour the rule breaks, but it is a change and it is why the finding is a suggestion rather than a warning.

rules.title: The capacity argument matches the default
rules.summary: `new List<T>(0)` and `new StringBuilder(16)` ask for the capacity the parameterless constructor already gives.
rules.rationale: A capacity argument is how an author records a measurement: this collection is known to hold about this many elements, so do not grow it from nothing. An argument equal to the type's own default records no measurement and makes no allocation smaller — it reads as a deliberate tuning decision to the next person, who then has to open the framework source to discover that it decides nothing. Removing it is a deletion with no runtime effect at all, which is the unusual case where the value is entirely in what the code no longer claims.

examples.bad:
var rows = new List<string>(0);
var text = new StringBuilder(16);
examples.good:
var rows = new List<string>();
var text = new StringBuilder();

rules.falsePositives: The constructor must be the framework's own single-`int` `capacity` overload on one of six types whose default is known and fixed — `List<T>`, `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`, `HashSet<T>`, `Queue<T>` and `Stack<T>` at 0, and `StringBuilder` at 16 — resolved through the semantic model and required to come from metadata rather than from source, so a same-named type of the author's own is never touched. The type must also expose an accessible parameterless constructor for the argument to be removable. ⚠ **Only a numeric literal is reported.** `new List<string>(DefaultCapacity)` is left alone even where the constant is 0: a named constant is a statement about intent that happens to equal the default today, and deleting it silently decouples the call site from the name. An argument list carrying a comment or a directive is left alone for the same reason. Any other capacity value, any other overload, and any other type are outside the rule.

rules.title: `GC.Collect` is called from application code
rules.summary: A forced collection suspends every thread and promotes what survives, so it usually makes the pressure it was added to relieve permanent.
rules.rationale: `GC.Collect` is almost always added after a memory graph looked wrong, and it is the one response that cannot help. The collector's generational assumption is that most objects die young; a collection forced at an arbitrary moment finds the young objects still live, promotes them to a longer-lived generation, and thereby guarantees that the next collection to reach them is a more expensive one. Meanwhile every managed thread is suspended for the duration. The cost is paid at every call and the benefit is a number in a profiler that looks better for one sample. What the call is standing in for is an allocation that should not happen, a buffer that should be pooled, or a handle that should be disposed — and none of those is an edit an analyzer can write, which is why this rule reports and does not fix.
rules.falsePositives: Every overload of `System.GC.Collect` is reported, resolved through the semantic model rather than matched on the written name. ⚠ **There is no fix**, and the rule says so in `rules.json` rather than offering the deletion: the call is a symptom, and removing it without dealing with what it was compensating for changes the program's memory behaviour in a direction nobody measured. ⚠ **Measurement code is the one legitimate caller and is excluded**: a method or type carrying a test or benchmark attribute — `Fact`, `Theory`, `Test`, `TestCase`, `TestMethod`, `Benchmark` and the BenchmarkDotNet setup and cleanup markers — establishes a known heap on purpose, and reporting there would be reporting the measurement rather than the program. A finaliser-behaviour test outside those attributes, and a deliberate collection at a genuine idle point in a desktop application, are real callers the rule still reports; they are the case for a suppression with a reason, which is what `SK7071` and the baseline are for.

rules.title: A thrown `NotImplementedException` has no issue reference
rules.summary: A member's body is `throw new NotImplementedException()` and nothing names the issue that owes the implementation.
rules.rationale: ⚠ This is `SK7040`'s requirement on the form that compiles, and it sits on Skala's premise rather than beside it. A model asked for an implementation produces a signature with a `throw new NotImplementedException()` body far more readily than it says it cannot do the work — and that body type-checks, binds, formats, and passes every analyzer in the build. It fails only when it runs, in a caller that had no way to know. A `TODO` at least announces itself to whoever opens the line; this announces itself to nobody. The requirement is therefore the same one `SK7040` makes: somewhere a reader will already be looking, name the issue that owns finishing this. The same vocabulary is accepted — a URL, `#123`, or a project key such as `SKALA-123` — read from the exception's own message, from the throw's own comments, or from the enclosing member's leading trivia.

examples.bad: public decimal Total(Order order) => throw new NotImplementedException();
examples.good:
// TODO SKALA-412: the discount table is not specified yet.
public decimal Total(Order order) => throw new NotImplementedException("SKALA-412");

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ Report-only, and deliberately so: no edit writes the implementation, and every mechanical guess available — delete the member, return `default`, change the exception type — turns a loud failure into a quiet one, which is strictly worse than what is there. Only a construction that is *thrown* is reported; Sonar's `S3717` tracks every use of the type, but constructing one to compare against or to hand to a test helper is not a member that compiles and does not work. ⚠ **`NotSupportedException` and `UnreachableException` never fire, and that is the rule's position rather than an omission.** Both are permanent statements about a contract — an operation this type will never offer, a branch the author asserts is unreachable — and they are what an author writes when the answer really is "not here". `NotImplementedException` is the one that means "not yet", and "not yet" is what needs an owner. A repository that uses source comments as its backlog should disable the rule, exactly as it would `SK7040`. ⚠ **Test doubles are the one class measured to fire in volume, and the rule does not exempt them.** Wrapped in a project file, three slices of `Testing/corpus/real/newtonsoft` produce nine findings, every one of them a member of a fake implementing an interface the test never calls; the corpus holds twelve such throws and not one carries a reference. The rule's position is that a fake noting that nothing calls the member is exactly the sentence the finding asks for, and a repository that disagrees should path-scope the severity to its test projects. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: The process is terminated outside the entry point
rules.summary: `Environment.Exit` is called somewhere other than the entry point, so the process ends without unwinding.
rules.rationale: `Environment.Exit` does not unwind. No `finally` runs, no `using` disposes, no buffered writer flushes and no `await` resumes. In a library, in a service, and in an executable's own helper class alike, it ends work that has nothing to do with whoever made the call — the caller's transaction is left open, its temporary file is left on disk, and its log line is left in a buffer that is never written.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The rule does not try to tell an application from a library, and that is a measurement rather than a shrug.** `LooseLoader` constructs its compilation with `OutputKind.DynamicallyLinkedLibrary`, so "this compilation is a library" and "no project file was loaded" are the same observation — and loose is the mode Skala exists for, because a folder of generated `.cs` files has no project. A rule keyed on `OutputKind` would report every console application analysed without its project file. The line drawn instead holds under every load mode: the entry point may end the process, because ending it is the process's own decision and there is nothing above to unwind into; everywhere else the call destroys cleanup somebody else wrote. The entry point is the compilation's own where there is one, and otherwise a `static Main` by name, which is the fallback loose mode needs. Top-level statements are the entry point and never fire. ⚠ `Environment.FailFast` is deliberately not reported: skipping cleanup is the whole point of it — it is what an author writes when the state is corrupt enough that running `finally` blocks is the more dangerous act — so reporting it would be reporting a decision rather than an accident. `Environment.ExitCode` is a property assignment, not a call, and never fires. The type is resolved by the semantic model and never matched on the written name. Report-only: the repair is to return, to throw, or to set an exit code and let the entry point end the process, and which of those the caller is owed is not something an edit can guess.

rules.title: The exception is both logged and rethrown
rules.summary: A `catch` hands the caught exception to a logging call and then rethrows it.
rules.rationale: Every layer that does this multiplies the log. One failure arrives as five entries with five different stack depths, nothing in any of them says they are the same event, and the layer that finally handled it is indistinguishable from the four that only watched it go past. Either handle the exception — and then it is not the caller's problem — or propagate it and let whoever handles it record it once.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The rule ships the half it can prove and the omitted half is named.** A finding requires the logging call to be handed *the caught exception itself*. Deciding that an arbitrary call "is logging" is name-matching, and name-matching a bare `logger.LogError("failed")` beside a `throw;` would report every method in the tree called `Error`; passing the caught exception to something in the logging vocabulary is not a guess, because nothing else does that. A `catch` with no exception variable therefore never fires, and neither does one that logs a message without the exception — under-reporting in the direction that keeps the rule usable. ⚠ **Wrapping is not rethrowing and is deliberately not reported.** `throw new ImportException(message, error)` translates the failure at a boundary and produces one record rather than two, and logging the original before translating it is how detail that the translation drops survives at all. Only a bare `throw;` and `throw error;` count — the two forms that send on the same exception the same layer just recorded. A nested `try`'s own `catch` is not this one: the walk is scoped to the clause that owns the node. Report-only: "handle it or propagate it" names two repairs, choosing between them is a decision about what this layer is for, and an edit that deleted the log would lose the context the log adds while one that deleted the `throw` would swallow a failure.

rules.title: The console is written to where a logger was meant
rules.summary: A `Console.Write` or `Console.WriteLine` is made from code that has a logger in scope.
rules.rationale: A console write cannot be filtered, routed, structured or correlated, and in every hosted environment — a container, a service, a function, a test host — it goes nowhere anybody looks. Complements `SK2016`, which assumes a logger is being used at all.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The rule does not decide whether this code is an application or a library, because nothing in the tree can tell it.** `LooseLoader` builds its compilation as `OutputKind.DynamicallyLinkedLibrary`, so "this is a library" and "no project file was loaded" are one observation, and loose is the mode Skala exists for. A rule keyed on `OutputKind` would report every line of every console application analysed without its project, which is `S106` turned into a false-positive engine. What ships is the narrower fact the issue's own title names and which no load mode can distort: **a logger is in scope at this call site and the code wrote to the console anyway** — a member or parameter typed `ILogger`, `ILogger<T>` or `ILog` is present, so the routing question is already answered for this code and answered differently two lines away. That is a contradiction inside one method rather than a policy judgement about the project. A console application's entry point printing usage has no logger and is never reported, which is the correct outcome by construction rather than by an exemption somebody has to maintain — and a service class that writes to the console and has no logger at all is under-reported, deliberately. The logger interface is matched on the type's own name and not on a namespace, because the namespace is the part that differs across `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging`, `Serilog`, `NLog` and `log4net`. `Console.Out` and `Console.Error` are reported through the receiver, so a `TextWriter` the caller handed in is not the console and never fires; reads such as `Console.ReadLine` never fire. Report-only: which level the line deserves is intent — `Debug`, `Information` and `Error` are all plausible for the same string — a console argument list is not mechanically a message template, and an edit that guessed would put the wrong severity on somebody's alerting.

rules.title: The collection's own method answers this faster than the LINQ extension
rules.summary: `List<T>` and `ImmutableList<T>` declare `Find`, `Exists` and `TrueForAll`; the `Enumerable` extension that answers the same question allocates an enumerator to do it.
rules.rationale: `FirstOrDefault`, `Any` and `All` are written against `IEnumerable<T>`, so they allocate an enumerator, drive it through `MoveNext` and call the predicate through it. `Find`, `Exists` and `TrueForAll` are members of the list, so they walk the backing array with an index and allocate nothing. The delegate is the same object under two names — `Predicate<T>` and `Func<T, bool>` have identical signatures — so the substitution costs the reader nothing either. `Any(x => x == v)` is a third case of the same argument and the sharpest: `Contains(v)` needs no delegate at all, and the comparison ends up somewhere the reader can see it.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Every pair was checked on the empty sequence, which is where a substitution like this goes wrong, and none of them changes a return.** `All` is vacuously `true` and `TrueForAll` returns `true` over zero elements; `Any` and `Exists` are both `false`; `FirstOrDefault` and `Find` both return `default(T)` — for a value type as well, so neither throws where the other does not. `First`, `Single` and `SingleOrDefault` are deliberately outside the table, because `Find` returns a default where those throw. ⚠ **The receiver must be `List<T>` or `ImmutableList<T>` as the semantic model resolves it**, never a type that merely has a member of the right name. A set carries an `IEqualityComparer<T>`, so `HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase).Contains(v)` and `Any(x => x == v)` genuinely disagree, and that is the false positive this restriction exists to prevent. ⚠ The `Any(x => x == v)` rewrite additionally requires an element type whose default equality comparer *is* its `==`: `string`, the integral types, `char`, `bool`, `decimal` and any `enum`. `double` and `float` are excluded because `NaN == NaN` is false where `EqualityComparer<double>.Default.Equals(NaN, NaN)` is true and `-0.0 == 0.0` is true where `Equals` is false; reference types are excluded because `==` may be identity, or an operator somebody wrote. The compared value must also be a name path or a literal, so that moving it out of the lambda does not change how many times it is evaluated. ⚠ The predicate must be written as a lambda or an anonymous method. A `Func<T, bool>` variable does not convert to `Predicate<T>` — the fix would be CS1503 — and a method group is left alone as the cheaper miss. ⚠ **One real behavioural difference is recorded rather than guarded**: `Enumerable.Any` iterates through the list's enumerator, which checks the version field, so a predicate that mutates the list mid-scan throws `InvalidOperationException`; `Exists` walks the array and does not. A predicate that mutates the collection it is scanning is a defect either way, and building a guard for it would mean proving a lambda pure.

rules.title: The loop looks up a key it is already holding
rules.summary: `foreach (var key in dict.Keys)` and then `dict[key]` in the body: the entry was already in hand and is hashed and probed for again, once per element.
rules.rationale: Enumerating `Keys` walks the same entries the dictionary would have handed over whole, and then throws the value away. Every `dict[key]` in the body hashes the key again, probes the bucket chain again and compares again — work the enumerator already did on the way past, multiplied by the count of the dictionary. Iterating the dictionary itself and deconstructing the pair is one pass with no hashing at all. `SK1033` reports the `ContainsKey`-then-index double lookup; this is the same waste inside a loop, which is where it is worth a `warning` rather than a suggestion.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The receiver is matched against a closed list of framework dictionaries** — `Dictionary`, `SortedDictionary`, `SortedList`, `ReadOnlyDictionary`, `ImmutableDictionary`, `ImmutableSortedDictionary` and `FrozenDictionary` — because the rewrite depends on `Keys` and the dictionary enumerating the same entries in the same order, and that is a promise those types make and `IDictionary<TKey, TValue>` does not. A user implementation whose `Keys` is a sorted projection would be reordered by the fix, so it is left alone. ⚠ **`ConcurrentDictionary` is excluded, and not only for tidiness**: its `Keys` takes every lock in the table and returns a snapshot, where iterating the table itself is a live, lock-free walk — under concurrent writes the two loops genuinely see different things, so the rewrite is a change to what the program observes rather than to what it costs. `SK4033` is where that receiver's costs are reported. ⚠ **A body that writes `dict[key] = …` withdraws the whole finding**, not just that site: the deconstructed `value` is a copy and assigning to it would silently stop updating the dictionary. So does a body that reassigns the dictionary variable, or passes it by reference. ⚠ The dictionary must be reached through a name path ending in a local, a parameter or a field. A property could hand back a different dictionary on the second read, and the fix leaves the indexer's receiver text in place precisely because it is not supposed to be re-evaluated. ⚠ The loop variable must be `var` or exactly the key type, and the fix needs a name for the value that the enclosing body does not already use; inside a `set` or `init` accessor `value` is taken by the implicit parameter, so a fallback name is chosen there rather than writing CS0136. ⚠ The rule is silent below C# 7.0 and where the framework's `KeyValuePair<TKey, TValue>` has no `Deconstruct`, because the fix would not compile.

rules.title: `Substring` is called to feed a search that takes a start index
rules.summary: `s.Substring(n).IndexOf(x)` copies the tail of the string onto the heap only to search inside it; `s.IndexOf(x, n)` reads the same characters in place.
rules.rationale: `Substring` is an allocation and a copy proportional to what is left of the string, and the only thing done with the result here is a search that already accepts the offset as an argument. `IndexOf(value, startIndex)` and `IndexOfAny(anyOf, startIndex)` begin exactly where the copy would have begun and never build it. `SK1028` makes the span-based version of the same argument; this one needs no new type at the call site at all, which is why it is the first thing to reach for.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The two expressions do not return the same number, and everything about this rule follows from that.** `s.Substring(n).IndexOf(x)` is an index into the copy; `s.IndexOf(x, n)` is an index into `s`; they differ by exactly `n`. So the finding is raised only where the result is used as a *presence test* — compared with `0` or `-1` by `>= 0`, `< 0`, `> -1`, `<= -1`, `== -1` or `!= -1`, in either operand order — because that is the one question both spellings answer identically. Where the number is assigned, returned, passed on, or compared with anything else, the rule is silent; a fix there would have been a silently wrong offset, which is worse than the allocation. ⚠ **`LastIndexOf` is excluded rather than overlooked**: its `startIndex` overload searches *backwards* from that position, so the substitution is not a narrower search but the opposite one. ⚠ Only the one-argument `Substring(n)` qualifies — `Substring(n, length)` bounds the search as well as moving its start, and the rewritten call would look past the end of what was asked for. ⚠ The start-index overload is looked up on the compilation's own `string` rather than assumed: `IndexOf(char, StringComparison)` exists and `IndexOf(char, int, StringComparison)` does not, so a rule that appended an `int` to whatever overload it saw would write a call that does not bind. ⚠ The offset and every search argument must be a literal or a path of names. Moving the offset after the arguments changes the evaluation order, and rather than reason about whose side effects could see whose, the rule declines when either side could have any. ⚠ The boundary cases were checked and agree: at `n == s.Length` both spellings answer "not found"; for an empty search string both answer "found" (at different positions, which is why only the presence test is offered); and both throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for the same out-of-range `n`. ⚠ `s.Substring(n).Contains(x)` is deliberately out of scope, because its rewrite turns a `bool` atom into a relational expression and that needs the surrounding-syntax analysis `SK1034` does for `Any()`.

rules.title: The `ConcurrentDictionary` member taken is the expensive one
rules.summary: `dict.Keys.Count` locks the whole table and copies every key into a new list to produce a number `dict.Count` already has; `dict.Count == 0` locks it to answer what `dict.IsEmpty` answers for free.
rules.rationale: On every other dictionary `Keys` and `Values` are views and `Count` is a field read. On this one they are neither. `ConcurrentDictionary.Keys` acquires every lock in the table and copies the whole collection into a fresh `List<TKey>` before the caller reads anything at all, so `dict.Keys.Count` is a locking O(n) allocation. `Count` acquires every lock as well, because a consistent total means stopping the table. `IsEmpty` acquires nothing and allocates nothing. The receiver is what makes the difference enormous rather than marginal, and it is invisible in the shape of the call — which is exactly why it is worth a rule.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **`SK1034` reads `dict.Keys.Count()` and offers `dict.Keys.Count`, which is right and leaves the expensive half standing.** This rule reports on the same span and declares `supersedes: ["SK1034"]`, so where both fire the stronger remedy wins and the weaker one stays in the report marked superseded rather than disappearing. Matching the span is the whole mechanism — `Supersession.Apply` pairs findings by rule, file, line and column — which is why `SK1034` runs inside this batch's own test list. The one shape where the two spans do not coincide is a mirrored comparison, `0 < dict.Keys.Count()`, where both are reported; both are true and neither is wrong. ⚠ **`dict.Keys.Contains(k)` looks like it belongs here and does not, and this is the useful exclusion.** `Keys` hands back a plain `List<TKey>`, whose `Contains` uses `EqualityComparer<TKey>.Default`, while `ContainsKey` uses the comparer the dictionary was *constructed* with. For a table built with `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` the two give different answers, and nothing at the call site says which kind of table this is — so the obvious rewrite is a behaviour change wearing a performance fix's clothes. ⚠ Only comparisons with `0`, or with `1` under `<`/`>=`, are read as emptiness tests; a count is never negative, so those are the only ones a comparison with a literal decides. Anything else is a claim about *how many*, which `IsEmpty` cannot answer. ⚠ `Any()` becomes `!dict.IsEmpty`, which is a unary expression where the call was a primary one, so it is offered only where the surrounding syntax cannot re-bind — the same restriction and the same list as `SK1034`. `dict.Keys.Any().ToString()` would otherwise become `!dict.IsEmpty.ToString()`, which parses, binds, and means something else. The `!dict.Keys.Any()` form has no such restriction, because `dict.IsEmpty` is primary too. ⚠ The receiver must be a path of names, since the fix writes it a second time. ⚠ `LongCount()` is left alone: it returns `long` where `Count` returns `int`, and a narrowing of the static type can change which overload a surrounding call resolves to.

rules.title: The collection is sorted before it is filtered
rules.summary: `xs.OrderBy(k).Where(p)` buffers, keys and sorts every element, and then throws some of them away; `xs.Where(p).OrderBy(k)` does all three to the survivors only.
rules.rationale: `OrderBy` is not lazy in the way the rest of the pipeline is: it buffers the entire sequence, computes a key for every element and sorts all of them before it yields the first one. Putting `Where` after it means paying `O(n log n)` on elements that are about to be discarded, and holding a buffer and a key array sized to the input rather than to the output. Swapping the two makes every one of those proportional to what survives — the one rewrite in this range that moves an asymptotic term rather than an allocation count.

examples.bad: var recent = entries.OrderBy(entry => entry.Created).Where(entry => entry.IsVisible);
examples.good: var recent = entries.Where(entry => entry.IsVisible).OrderBy(entry => entry.Created);

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The output sequence is identical, and that rests entirely on `OrderBy` being a stable sort.** A stable sort leaves elements with equal keys in their original relative order and `Where` preserves relative order, so both spellings emit the survivors ordered by key with ties broken by source position. LINQ documents `OrderBy` as stable; were it not, the two orders would differ for equal keys and this rule would be wrong. ⚠ **The indexed `Where(Func<T, int, bool>)` overload is refused.** After the sort the index is a position in sorted order and before it a position in source order, so moving that call rewrites the program rather than the pipeline. A parameter count alone would not tell the two overloads apart — the predicate's shape is what does. ⚠ `Queryable` is excluded for the reason `SK4010` excludes it: a provider is free to translate one ordering of a pipeline and not the other, and a fix that turns a working query into a runtime "unsupported expression" is worse than the sort it saved. ⚠ **What does change is when the two functions run and on what.** The predicate is now invoked in source order rather than in sorted order, and the key selector runs only on the survivors — so a key selector that throws for an element the filter would have removed used to throw and now does not, and a predicate with side effects observes a different order. Both are defects in the lambda rather than in the rewrite, and neither is decidable without proving a lambda pure. ⚠ **The static type of the whole expression widens from `IEnumerable<T>` to `IOrderedEnumerable<T>`.** Every context that accepted the first accepts the second, but a `var` declaration now infers the ordered type and an overload set containing both could resolve differently. ⚠ Where the `Where` is immediately consumed by one of `SK4010`'s nine operators, this rule says nothing: both are right about `xs.OrderBy(k).Where(p).First()` and their edits overlap, so `SK4010` keeps it — folding the predicate into `First` lets the search stop at the first match, and once applied this shape no longer exists. ⚠ A `ThenBy` between the two calls is not this shape and is not reported, because the `Where` receiver is then the `ThenBy` rather than the sort.

rules.title: A type is declared in the global namespace
rules.summary: The global namespace is one flat name table shared with every referencing assembly, and it is the one namespace a `using` cannot name.
rules.rationale: A namespace is how a type says which program it belongs to, and the global namespace says nothing. Every assembly in a consumer's dependency closure contributes to the same flat table, so two libraries that each declare a global `Settings` cannot both be referenced — and the error arrives in the consumer's build, naming two types the consumer did not write. The usual escapes do not apply: `using Configuration = Contoso.Configuration;` needs a namespace to alias, and `global::Settings` names the ambiguity rather than resolving it, so the only repair available downstream is an `extern alias` on the whole assembly. The namespace costs one line here; omitting it moves the cost to somebody who cannot pay it without a source change to a package they do not own.
rules.falsePositives:
**Only a declaration whose direct parent is the compilation unit.** A nested type takes its container's namespace, so it is never reported — the finding belongs to the outer type and reporting it again per member would multiply one mistake by the size of the file. A declaration inside a `namespace` block or a file-scoped namespace has a namespace node above it and is out of scope by construction.

**A `file` type is never reported.** `file sealed class Helper { }` is visible only inside the file that declares it, so it is in the global namespace and in nobody's way — which is exactly what the modifier is for. It is the one shape where "no namespace" is the correct answer rather than an omission.

⚠ **A type named `Program` is exempt, and that is not a courtesy.** A file with top-level statements gets a compiler-generated `Program` in the global namespace, and `public partial class Program { }` — the documented way to make an entry point visible to `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` — has to be in the global namespace too, or it declares a *different* type and the test host cannot find the program. There is no namespace that declaration could be moved to, so a finding on it would name no available repair. The cost is that a genuinely stray type called `Program` goes unreported.

**Every type kind is reported, including `enum` and `delegate`.** They occupy the same name table as a class and collide in exactly the same way; excluding them would make the rule's silence mean two different things.

**Generated code is excluded**, the same as every rule in this range: a global type written by a source generator is the generator's decision and not the author's.

**The finding is real and harmless in an application that ships no reference surface.** An executable nobody references cannot collide with anything, and a console program with one global helper class is a shape the rule reports and a reviewer may reasonably baseline. The rule cannot tell an application from a library — the output kind is an MSBuild property and not a fact about a syntax tree — and the general case is a library, so the rule reports and says so here.

⚠ **No fix, and the reason is that the edit needs a name nobody has written down.** Wrapping the file in a namespace is a mechanical two-span edit *once the namespace is known*, and it is not: deriving it from the folder path requires the project's root namespace and the path the project treats as its root, neither of which an analyzer can see, and inventing one would put a name into a public API on a guess. `hasFix: false` is a decision, not an omission.

rules.title: `readonly` does not protect a mutable field's contents
rules.summary: `readonly` constrains the field and never the object in it, so a non-private array or mutable collection is writable by every caller that can see it.
rules.rationale: `public readonly string[] Names` stops `Names = …` and stops nothing else. Every caller can still write `Names[0] = "…"`, and on a `List<T>` can `Clear()` it — from another thread, at any time, with no compiler complaint anywhere. What makes this worse than declaring the field without the modifier is the reader: `readonly` is the keyword C# has for "this does not change", so a reviewer who sees it stops looking for the mutation, and static analysis, code review and the type's own documentation all inherit the mistake. A field that must not be written through is either `private` with a `IReadOnlyList<T>` property over it, or typed as something that really is immutable — `ImmutableArray<T>`, `FrozenDictionary<K, V>`, `ReadOnlyCollection<T>`. `readonly` is neither of those and cannot be made into either by adding a keyword.
rules.falsePositives:
⚠ **The mutable types are an explicit list, and an interface test would have been wrong.** The obvious implementation asks whether the field's type implements `ICollection<T>` — and `ImmutableArray<T>`, `ImmutableList<T>` and `ReadOnlyCollection<T>` all implement `IList<T>`, explicitly, throwing `NotSupportedException` from every mutator. That implementation reports the immutable collections this rule's own advice tells somebody to switch to, which is the worst answer available. So the rule matches a named set — arrays, `List`/`Dictionary`/`HashSet`/`SortedSet`/`SortedList`/`SortedDictionary`/`Queue`/`Stack`/`LinkedList`, `Collection<T>` and `ObservableCollection<T>`, the four mutable generic interfaces, and the non-generic `ArrayList`/`Hashtable`/`IList`/`IDictionary`/`ICollection` — resolved through the semantic model, never by the written name. **The cost is a miss on a user-defined mutable type**, and that is the right direction for a rule whose whole risk is over-firing.

⚠ **Concurrent collections are deliberately absent.** `public readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, int> Cache` is the *correct* declaration for a shared cache: the type exists to be written through by many callers at once, so the field being non-reassignable is the whole of what anybody expected `readonly` to mean there. Reporting it would be reporting a design for working as designed. The same argument does not extend to `List<T>`, which promises nothing about concurrent writers.

**A private field is never reported, however mutable it is.** The declaring type owns its own state, and `readonly` there is a note to the type's own author rather than a promise made to anybody else. `internal` and `private protected` *are* reported: both hand the object to code the declaration cannot see, and "the rest of my assembly" is still somebody else at three in the morning.

**A zero-length array is exempt.** `public static readonly string[] Empty = [];` has no element anyone could write, so `readonly` really is the whole guarantee. The three ways to say it — a `[]` collection expression, `Array.Empty<T>()` and `new T[0]` — are all read out of the initializer, per declarator, so `readonly int[] a = [], b;` reports `b` and leaves `a` alone.

**A read-only declared type is silence, and that is a known hole.** A field typed `IReadOnlyList<T>` is not reported even when it holds a `List<T>` that a caller could cast back to and mutate. The rule reads declarations, and that declaration says read-only; catching the cast is a dataflow question about every holder of the value, which is a different rule in a different band.

**An unresolved type is silence.** If the field's type binds to an error type the rule says nothing, because "not a mutable collection" and "the compilation could not tell" are the same answer from a naive test and only one of them is a finding. This is why the rule is semantic and does not run under `--load=loose`.

**Only arrays and collections, not mutability in general.** A `public readonly StringBuilder Log` has the same defect and is not reported: widening the rule to every mutable object would need a definition of "mutable" that C# does not have, and the collections are where the mistake is both common and unambiguous.

⚠ **No fix.** The three repairs — change the field's type, make it private and add a read-only property, or drop `readonly` and admit the field is mutable — are three different decisions about a public API, and two of them break every caller.
