rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The rewrite evaluates the receiver once where the original evaluated it twice, and that is stated rather than hidden.** On a property whose getter is not idempotent the two programs differ; property paths are admitted anyway, for the reason `RewriteGuards.IsPlainNamePath` gives — excluding them would silence the rule on `this.Items` and `Options.Map`, which is most of its value, and the two reads it collapses are adjacent inside one expression. An invocation, an indexer or an `await` anywhere in the *receiver* is refused, because there the second evaluation is visibly a second call. ⚠ **The accessed member must be a reference type and must already be the conditional's own type.** `x != null ? x.Count : null` is a target-typed `int?` and `x?.Count` is an `int?` arrived at differently; matching them would mean reasoning about the conversion the expression was subjected to, and being wrong about it changes an overload. ⚠ A receiver that is already the subject of a `?.` — `x != null ? x?.Y : null` — is refused rather than rewritten, because appending the suffix would produce `x??.Y`; so is `x != null ? x() : null`, where `x?()` is not syntax. ⚠ A null comparison whose operand type declares `operator ==` is left alone, since `==` there is not the null test `?.` performs, and the whole finding is withheld inside an expression tree, where `?.` is CS8072. ⚠ **The declared floor is C# 7 and `?.` arrived in C# 6**: the version map Skala checks floors against starts at C# 7, so the floor is stated one version high rather than falling through to `preview`.

rules.title: Use a discard
rules.summary: A named local that exists only to receive a value nobody reads — a return value kept for the call's effect, or an `out var` the caller does not want.
rules.rationale: A name is a claim that something will be referred to again. When nothing refers to it, the name is a small lie the reader has to check: they look for the second use, do not find it, and only then know the call was there for its effect. `_` says that in the first character, and it says it to the compiler too — the local stops being allocated and stops being something a later edit can accidentally read.

examples.bad: var ignored = queue.TryDequeue(out var unused);
examples.good: _ = queue.TryDequeue(out _);

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **This is not `SK0217`.** `arrange-discard-declaration` decides how an *existing* discard is spelled — `var _` against `_` — and never introduces one; this rule introduces one and never restyles one, so the two do not double-count. ⚠ **`_` is a discard only where nothing else claims the name.** A local, a parameter or a field called `_` turns `_ = Foo();` into an assignment to that thing, silently, so every lookup for `_` at the rewrite position must come back empty. ⚠ **Only `out var`, never `out T`.** A discard has no type, so replacing an explicitly typed out-variable can change which overload a call resolves to; `out var` is already typeless in that sense and loses nothing. ⚠ The local's initializer must be a call, a construction, an `await` or a conditional access — something whose *evaluation* is the reason the statement exists. `var x = 5;` is dead code whose repair is deletion, and `_ = 5;` is the same dead code with an assignment bolted on. ⚠ "Never read" is measured as "never mentioned" over the whole member, deliberately: a later assignment is not a read, but dropping a declaration underneath one is a compile error rather than a tidy-up, and a local written twice and read never has no fix here either way. ⚠ `using`, `await using`, `const`, `ref`, attributed and multi-declarator declarations are all left alone.

rules.title: Inline the `out` variable declaration
rules.summary: A bare local declaration whose only purpose is the `out` argument in the statement below it.
rules.rationale: The inline form has been available since C# 7 and the separated form is still what a model writes, because most of its training data predates it. The separated form also states a lie for one statement: `int value;` claims a variable exists and is meaningful before anything has put a value in it, and a reader has to look down one line to find out that it does not. `SK1033` already reports the `TryGetValue` shape this most often appears in.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The written type is carried across verbatim and never replaced by `var`.** `out` is invariant, so the declared type is exactly the parameter's and reproducing it leaves overload resolution where it was, while `out var` is typeless in that respect and can move it; copying the text rather than the symbol also keeps an alias or a `using`-shortened name spelled the way the file spells it. ⚠ **Scope is the whole risk and it is answered by position, not by a table of statement kinds.** An expression variable is scoped no wider than the statement introducing it, so every reference to the local must be inside the statement the `out` argument belongs to, and the argument must sit in that statement's own expression — not inside a nested block, a lambda or a local function, each of which would put the new declaration somewhere the old one was not. ⚠ The declaration must be immediately above, must have no initializer, and must be a single declarator with no modifiers and no attributes; exactly one `out` argument may name the local, since two would be two declarations of one name. A `ref` argument is not an `out` argument and is left alone.

rules.title: The `lock` is taken over a synchronization primitive
rules.summary: A `lock` statement is taken over an object that is itself a synchronization primitive — a `SemaphoreSlim`, a `ReaderWriterLockSlim`, or anything below `WaitHandle`.
rules.rationale: Every reference type carries a monitor, so `lock (semaphore)` compiles. It gives the author a monitor they did not mean, taken over an object whose own waiting happens somewhere else entirely: a thread parked inside `semaphore.Wait()` holds nothing the monitor knows about, and a thread inside `lock (semaphore)` excludes nobody who calls `Wait`. The two mechanisms do not compose, and where the primitive takes its own monitor internally the mistake is a deadlock rather than a no-op. The code above it reads as though the object were guarded, which is the expensive part.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Fixless, and not for want of trying.** The repair is to decide which mechanism the code meant — take the primitive properly, or introduce a separate lock object — and no edit can choose between those without knowing what the other threads do. Rewriting `lock (semaphore) { … }` into `semaphore.Wait()/Release()` changes which threads are excluded, and introducing a new field changes the type's shape; both are design decisions. ⚠ **This is not `SK1023` and never overlaps it.** `SK1023` looks at a private `readonly object` field whose only use is as a lock target and modernizes a lock that is already correct; this rule never fires on `object`, so the two are disjoint by the lock target's type. ⚠ **`System.Threading.Lock` is excluded explicitly** — it is a synchronization primitive and it is also the one type a C# 13 `lock` statement is supposed to be taken over, since the compiler lowers it to `Lock.EnterScope` rather than to `Monitor`; reporting it would contradict `SK1023`'s own fix. ⚠ The type is resolved from the compilation and never matched on the written name: `Semaphore` and `Barrier` are plausible names for somebody's own type. ⚠ **Stated scope limit:** the rule matches the `lock` statement only. `Monitor.Enter(semaphore)` is the same mistake spelled without the keyword and is not reported, because deciding that the matching `Exit` runs on every path is a different analysis; the negative fixture set records that rather than hiding it. `lock (this)` and `lock (someCollection)` are their own arguments and are not this one.

rules.title: The compound operation on a `volatile` field is not atomic
rules.summary: `++`, `--` or a compound assignment is applied to a `volatile` field, which is a read and a write and not one operation.
rules.rationale: `volatile` buys visibility and orders nothing else. The read and the write of `counter++` are still two instructions with a window between them, so two threads read the same value and one update is lost — exactly as they would without the keyword. What makes this worth a warning rather than a hint is the keyword itself: it is the mark of an author who thought about threading and concluded wrongly, so the next reader trusts the field and does not look again.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Fixless, and the issue proposing it asked for a fix.** Four separate obstacles, each of which alone is enough: (1) `Interlocked.Increment(ref field)` on a `volatile` field is **CS0420** — a `ref` to a volatile field is not treated as volatile — so the obvious edit puts a compiler warning into code that had none; (2) `f++` as an *expression* yields the value before the increment and `Interlocked.Increment` yields the value after, so only the expression-statement position is rewritable at all; (3) `|=`, `&=` have an `Interlocked` form only on recent frameworks, `^=` has none, and `*=`, `/=`, `<<=` have none anywhere; (4) the honest repair — drop `volatile` and route every access through `Interlocked`/`Volatile` — changes the field's contract and touches every other access to it, including accesses in other files. `hasFix: false` states that rather than guessing. ⚠ **The rule withdraws inside a `lock`.** `volatile` beside a monitor is redundant, not wrong, and the update under the monitor is atomic; a finding there would send a reader to threading code that is correct. ⚠ **It withdraws in a constructor**, where no other thread can hold a reference to the instance yet — but *not* through a lambda written in one, because a delegate runs whenever somebody invokes it. ⚠ **Stated scope limit:** `Monitor.Enter` and a semaphore held across the statement are the same guarantee spelled without the keyword and are not recognised, so a field updated under one of those is reported. Deciding that the matching release runs on every path is a dataflow question this rule does not ask; the miss is a false positive rather than a silence, and the negative fixture set records it. `volatile` cannot be applied to `long`, `double` or `decimal`, so the widest-window cases of this bug cannot carry the keyword and are outside the rule by construction.

rules.title: The double-checked locking is not correct
rules.summary: A check-lock-check initialization reads its field outside the lock and the field is not `volatile`.
rules.rationale: The idiom exists to skip the lock on the common path, and the read it skips the lock for is the outer one. Without `volatile` nothing orders that read against the writes the constructor performed, so a second thread can see a non-null reference to an object whose fields it cannot see yet, and use it. The lock is real, the inner check is real, and the object is still half-built. ⚠ It works on x86 and x64 by accident of those processors' ordering and stops working on ARM64, which is where a great deal of .NET now runs — so this is not a fragile shape, it is a shape with a platform on which it is already wrong.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Fixless.** Adding `volatile` looks like a one-word edit and is not one: it changes the field's memory contract for every access in the program, costs a fence on every read of a field that may be read in a loop, and is only one of three defensible repairs — the others being `Lazy<T>` (see `SK3009`) and dropping the outer check for an unconditional lock. Choosing among those is a design decision. ⚠ **The shape is gated four ways and all four must hold**: the outer condition is the *whole* condition and a plain field reference tested for null (or `!flag` on a `bool` field); its body runs a `lock`; the lock body holds a second check of the *same* field; and that second branch publishes the field with a plain assignment. `Volatile.Read(ref f) == null` fails the first gate and `Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref f, …)` fails the last, which is how code that has already done the ordering by hand stays silent. ⚠ **Reference types and `bool` only.** The finding's advice is "make it `volatile`", and CS0677 makes that illegal for `long`, `double`, `decimal` and any user struct, so on those the message would name a repair that does not compile. ⚠ **The field must be declared in source**, because a field from another assembly cannot be made `volatile` by anybody reading the finding. ⚠ **Two of the three ReSharper inspections named in the proposing issue are not covered**: `PossibleMultipleWriteAccessInDoubleCheckLocking` and `ReadAccessInDoubleCheckLocking` both turn on distinguishing `f = new Foo(); f.Init();` from `var t = new Foo(); t.Init(); f = t;`, and separating those from a harmless `return f;` in the same branch needs a rule about *which* reads publish. Stated rather than approximated. ⚠ A single-threaded type that happens to be written this way is reported; the idiom's whole point is threading, so the shape is its own claim about intent.

rules.title: Locks are taken in inconsistent orders
rules.summary: One type nests the same two lock fields inside each other in both orders, which is the textbook deadlock.
rules.rationale: Two paths that take the same pair of locks in opposite orders deadlock the moment both run. It survives review because the two halves are almost never on the same screen: each method reads as a perfectly ordinary pair of nested locks, and only the two together are wrong. Nothing in Roslyn or the `CA*` set reports it. The analysis is a lock *order* and nothing more — every `lock` whose target is a field of the type contributes an ordered pair for each lock it is nested inside, and a pair present in both directions is the finding.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Fixless, and unusually clearly so.** No edit decides which lock should be taken first: choosing the hierarchy is the design decision the type failed to make, and swapping the order in the method the tool happened to see second is as likely to be the wrong half as the right one. ⚠ **Only two lock-target spellings are accepted: a bare identifier and `this.field`, both resolving to a field of the type under analysis.** Everything else — a local, a parameter, `peer.gate` — is opaque, and ⚠ **that is a recall decision and not a soundness one**, which is easy to mistake and was mistaken in this rule's first draft. A cycle over two fields reached through two different instances is a real deadlock, the classic bank-transfer one, and this rule does not report it. The reason is the message rather than the analysis: a finding names fields and not objects, so "`history` while holding `balance`" would be an ambiguous sentence about which account each name meant. Widening the rule needs an answer to that, and the negative fixture set records the miss under that name rather than filing it as a false positive avoided. An opaque target is not fatal to the locks around it: it contributes no pair and does not break pairs recorded across it, because `lock (a) { lock (opaque) { lock (b) } }` still takes `a` before `b`. ⚠ **The nesting walk stops at a lambda or a local function.** A delegate written inside a `lock` body does not run inside it, so treating the enclosing lock as held would invent an order the program does not have — and the invented pair is what would produce the finding. ⚠ **A re-entrant `lock (a) { lock (a) }` is not a pair**: a monitor is recursive for the thread that holds it. ⚠ **The unit is the symbol, not the file**, which is why the rule is `scope: Compilation` and uncached: issue #56's whole argument is that the two halves are rarely in the same file. ⚠ **Instance fields make the finding conditional on the instance.** Two threads on *different* objects take `a` and `b` of their own object and do not deadlock; the finding is a claim about the type's lock hierarchy, and a type that means two instances never interact has said so nowhere. A static pair has no such caveat. ⚠ `Monitor.Enter` is not a `lock` statement and contributes nothing, so a type that mixes the two can hide half of a pair.

rules.title: The field is guarded on some paths and not others
rules.summary: A private field is written without the type's one lock, and is accessed under that lock at least twice elsewhere.
rules.rationale: A field taken under a lock in nine places and written bare in the tenth is a race that testing will not find: the tenth path is usually the one added last and the window is usually nanoseconds wide. The analysis is which lock, if any, is held at each access — the same analysis `SK3043` needs, computed across the whole type rather than one file.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Fixless.** Wrapping the offending statement in the lock is one repair and taking the lock at the caller is another, and which one is right depends on what else the caller does between the two — an edit that guesses can introduce a nested lock or a lock held across an I/O call. ⚠ **The rule is deliberately far narrower than its title, and the gates are the rule.** docs/plan/16 § R3: a wrong concurrency finding sends somebody to read threading code that was correct, which is the most expensive reading there is, so every gate below buys precision at the cost of recall knowingly. **(1)** The type must have *exactly one* lock object and every `lock` in it must be taken over that one field; two gates is a hierarchy and which one guards a given field is not decidable from the shape. **(2)** The type must use no other synchronization at all — no `Interlocked`, `Volatile`, `Monitor`, semaphore, reader-writer lock or `Lazy` — because any of those is ordering the rule cannot see and would call an access unguarded. That list is matched on the written name, which is right here for once: it can only silence the rule, so a collision with somebody's own `Monitor` costs a finding and never produces a wrong one. **(3)** The unguarded access must be a *write*. A bare read of an otherwise-guarded field is a real hazard and is also the shape of a deliberate best-effort snapshot — `public int Count => count;` — and the two are not distinguishable here. **(4)** The write must sit in a member that is callable from outside the type and that the type never calls from inside the lock; a private helper, or a public method the type itself only invokes while holding the lock, is the "caller holds the lock" contract and is extremely common. `Dispose` is excluded by name, because disposal after the last user has let go is the normal contract. **(5)** Any access to the field inside a lambda or a local function withdraws the field entirely: a delegate runs whenever somebody invokes it, holding whatever they hold. **(6)** At least two guarded accesses are required — one guarded and one bare is as likely to be a lock introduced in the wrong place as one forgotten in the other. ⚠ **Silence is not a claim.** A field this rule says nothing about is a field it could not decide, not a field it believes is synchronized.

rules.title: The inheritance chain is deeper than the threshold
rules.summary: A class declares more base classes above it, within this compilation's own source, than dotnet_code_quality.SK7080.threshold (default 4).
rules.rationale: Every level above a class is a place a member can come from and a place behaviour can be changed without touching the file in front of the reader. The number is worth reporting only for the part of the chain the repository actually wrote: `MyControl : Button` is one decision somebody made, and the eight framework types above `Button` are not. So the count stops at the first base class this compilation did not declare — which is also why the default is 4 rather than the textbook 5 or 6, since a chain of four source-declared bases is already unusual. Flattening a hierarchy is a design change with no mechanical form, so there is no fix.
rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off — so the default is set above what the reference trees contain and the threshold is an .editorconfig option. ⚠ **The chain stops at the first base class not declared in this compilation's source.** A framework base contributes 1 and its own ancestors contribute nothing: depth from a framework is not a decision anybody in the repository can act on, and counting it would make the rule an opinion about which framework to use. ⚠ The same rule makes the count *under*-report across an assembly boundary — a base class in a referenced project is metadata here — which is the safe direction and is why the number is described as "within this compilation's own source". ⚠ **An unresolved base type withdraws the measurement entirely**: a chain that cannot be walked reads as depth 1, and reporting the smaller number would be silent rather than wrong. That is also why the rule produces nothing on a source slice with no dependency closure (issue #277) — the shape is present and the analysis correctly declines. Only classes and record classes are measured; an interface has a graph rather than a chain, and a struct has no base chain to walk. Generated code is excluded. A partial class is reported once, on the part that carries the base list.

rules.title: The type depends on more other types than the threshold
rules.summary: One type declaration mentions more distinct other named types than dotnet_code_quality.SK7081.threshold (default 80).
rules.rationale: This is the metric `SK7001`–`SK7006` do not carry. A type can be short, shallow and simple in every one of them and still know about forty other types, and every one of those forty is a reason this file has to be reopened when something else changes. Counting the distinct named types a declaration mentions — bases, member types, locals, constructions, static receivers, attributes and the arguments of the generics it names — measures how much of the design has to be held in mind at once to change it, which is what people mean when they say a class is entangled. ⚠ The default of 80 is deliberately far above the textbook 30: on Skala's own tree — which is a Roslyn analyzer host, and therefore names one type per syntax-node kind before it does anything — a threshold of 30 fires on 125 type declarations and 80 fires on six, and those six are the god objects a reader would name unprompted. Reporting the shoulder of the distribution rather than its tail is the "useless" outcome this family's rationale names. Splitting a type is a design change with no mechanical form, so there is no fix.

examples.bad: // one class that names forty other types across its fields, parameters and locals
examples.good: // the same work behind two or three collaborators, each naming its own handful

rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off — so the default is set above what the reference trees contain and the threshold is an .editorconfig option. ⚠ **Special types are not counted.** `int`, `string`, `object`, `void`, `IEnumerable<T>` and the rest of the language's own vocabulary would add the same handful to every type in the repository and separate nothing. ⚠ **The type itself, anything nesting it, and anything it nests are not counted**: a type that organises itself with nested helpers is not coupled to somebody else's design, and the file a reader opens contains both. ⚠ **A nested type is not descended into** — it has its own declaration and its own measurement, and charging the outer type for the inner one's dependencies would report the same union once per level. ⚠ **An unresolved reference is skipped rather than counted**, which under-reports; on a source slice with no dependency closure (issue #277) it under-reports to nothing, so a zero from this rule on such a tree says the analysis declined and not that the types are decoupled. Measured per *declaration*, like `SK7004`, so a partial type is measured once per file — which is the file a person opens. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: The conditional expressions are nested
rules.summary: Conditional expressions nest more deeply than dotnet_code_quality.SK7082.threshold (default 1), counting a right-associated ladder as one level.
rules.rationale: Nested `?:` is the one expression form where operator precedence and reader expectation reliably disagree: `a ? b : c ? d : e` groups one way and `a ? b ? c : d : e` another, and neither grouping is visible without counting. ⚠ The measurement makes one distinction that decides whether the rule is usable at all: a right-associated ladder — `a ? x : b ? y : z` — costs **one** level, not one per rung. That shape is an `else if` chain written as an expression; it reads top to bottom, each condition is tested once, and charging it per rung would make the rule fire on the one nested form that is idiomatic. What costs a level is a `?:` anywhere else inside another: in the condition, in the `true` branch, or buried inside the `false` branch rather than being it. Rewriting a nest is a judgement about which branch deserves a name, so there is no fix.

examples.bad: var label = ready ? (loud ? "READY" : "ready") : "waiting";

rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. ⚠ **The right-associated ladder is exempt and that exemption is the rule.** Without it the default threshold would fire on `n < 10 ? "small" : n < 100 ? "medium" : "large"`, which no reader has ever had trouble with, and the category would be switched off within a day. Parentheses around a ladder rung do not change the number, because some house styles write them and some do not. ⚠ A lambda body restarts the count, exactly as `SK7006`'s nesting depth does: `xs.Select(x => x > 0 ? a : b)` written inside a conditional is not a nested conditional in any sense a reader experiences. ⚠ **An interpolation hole restarts it too, and for the rule's own reason.** The rule exists because precedence and reader expectation disagree about `?:`; inside `$"…{…}…"` they cannot, because the hole has explicit delimiters and C# *requires* a conditional written in one to be parenthesised — a bare `:` there is the format specifier. There is nothing left to mis-group. ⚠ Only the outermost conditional of a nest reports — every conditional in the compilation reaches the analyzer, and reporting each would produce one finding per level pointing at the same expression, with the innermost carrying the smallest number. A null-conditional `?.` and a null-coalescing `??` are different operators and are not counted. Generated code is excluded. The finding points at the outermost `?` token.

rules.title: The string literal is repeated
rules.summary: One string literal is written in a file more times than dotnet_code_quality.SK7083.threshold (default 5), counting only literals at least dotnet_code_quality.SK7083.minimum_length characters long (default 5) that contain a letter.
rules.rationale: The same literal in several places is the same rename waiting to be done incompletely — the argument `nameof` makes for member names, applied to keys, formats and messages. ⚠ **It takes two options, and the second is what makes it usable.** A repeat count on its own reports `", "`, `"/"` and `"true"` long before it reports anything worth extracting, so a minimum length holds the floor and a literal must also contain a letter: a repeated separator or punctuation run is not a name anybody was going to give. ⚠ The default count is 5 — a literal must be written six times in one file — and that is the conservative end of a measurement with no wrong answer. On Skala's own tree a count of 3 reports 144 literals and a count of 5 reports 64; every one of the 144 is a real repeat, and the ones the higher default drops are the HTML fragments and fixture file names nobody was going to extract. The count is the option a repository lowers rather than raises, so the shipped number is the one that leaves room to. Choosing the name is the whole of the work, so there is no fix.

examples.bad:
logger.LogWarning("tenant-id header missing");
// … and "tenant-id" written again in three other places in the same file
examples.good: const string TenantIdHeader = "tenant-id";

rules.falsePositives: A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. ⚠ **The minimum length and the letter test are the rule**, not decoration: without them the default count reports every separator and every one-word flag in the repository. ⚠ **A `const` initialiser is not counted** — it is the repair, and a rule that still fires after somebody did exactly what it asked is the fastest way to teach people it is noise. ⚠ **An attribute argument is not counted**: it must be a compile-time constant, so the only extraction available is a `const` the attribute then names, and the ones that actually repeat are test display names, obsolescence messages and route templates, where writing the string out at the declaration is the point. ⚠ **Counted per file, and per file deliberately.** The scope where a repeat is visible and a `const` is an obvious repair is the one a reader has open; counting per compilation would report a literal shared by two unrelated files, where the repair is a shared constant nobody has a place for and the finding points at neither site. One finding per literal, at the first occurrence — one per site would report the same decision as many times as it was made. Interpolated strings are not literals and their text is not counted; neither are UTF-8 literals, which are a different expression kind. Comparison is ordinal on the literal's value, so a verbatim and a regular spelling of the same text count together. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: Integer division feeds a fractional result
rules.summary: A division evaluated in an integral type is converted to float, double or decimal, so the fractional part is discarded before the conversion that asks for it.
rules.rationale: Asking for a fractional type is the author saying the fraction matters, and integral division has already thrown it away by the time the conversion runs. The truncation happens inside the operator, not at the assignment, so nothing in the surrounding code shows it. ⚠ The finding is independent of the checked context: no overflow is involved and the result is the same whether the project sets CheckForOverflowUnderflow or not. The fix casts the dividend to the fractional type, which changes the computed value — that is the point, and it is why the fix is not safe to apply unreviewed.

examples.bad: double ratio = hits / total;
examples.good: double ratio = (double)hits / total;

rules.falsePositives: Only built-in, non-lifted division whose result type is a fixed-width integral type is considered, and only where the result reaches float, double or decimal — either by conversion or through a cast written immediately around the division. ⚠ Roslyn does not report a cast's target as the operand's converted type, so `(double)(a / b)` is invisible to the conversion test and is matched by reading the enclosing cast instead; a rule that checked only the conversion would miss the commonest wrong repair for this defect while looking complete. ⚠ An explicit cast of the division to an *integral* type — `(long)(a / b)` in a double context — is read as the author saying truncation is intended, and is not reported; it is the documented way to keep the shape and silence the rule. Division by a constant 1 or -1, and a constant zero dividend, are exact and are not reported: the shape is present and no fraction is lost. Native integers, nullable operands, user-defined operators, dynamic and generic type parameters are excluded. The rule does not decide whether truncation was wrong, only that it happened before a fractional type was asked for.

rules.title: The arithmetic has a result its constant operand already fixes
rules.summary: A built-in integral arithmetic or bitwise operation has a constant operand that makes the operation either the identity or a constant.
rules.rationale: `x * 1`, `x | 0` and `x & 0` compute nothing. Written by hand they are usually the residue of an edit that removed the interesting operand, and written by a model they are usually a placeholder that was never filled in — which is why the range matters more for generated code than for code somebody typed. ⚠ Every case reported here holds identically in a checked and an unchecked context: an identity cannot overflow and a constant result cannot either, so the project's CheckForOverflowUnderflow setting never changes the answer.

examples.bad: var scaled = weight * 1;
examples.good: var scaled = weight;

rules.falsePositives: Only built-in, non-lifted `+ - * / % & | ^` whose result type is a fixed-width integral type is considered, and the non-constant operand's type must equal that result type — so `someByte * 1` is left alone, because removing the operator would change the expression's static type and a `var` target with it. ⚠ Floating point is excluded on purpose: `x + 0.0` is not the identity, because it turns negative zero into positive zero. `0 - x` is negation, not an identity, and is not reported. Where the operation has a constant result rather than an identity — `x & 0`, `x % 1`, `x | -1` — the other operand must be a plain local, parameter or non-volatile field reference, so that discarding its evaluation cannot discard a side effect; anything else is left alone rather than reported without a fix. Compound assignment (`x *= 1`), shifts (which SK2052 owns), enums, pointers, decimal, `Math.Clamp` with an inverted range and cross-file constant dependencies are all outside this initial scope.

rules.title: The shift count is masked to a different count
rules.summary: A shift's constant count is outside the range of its promoted left operand's width, so C# masks it and the expression shifts by a different amount.
rules.rationale: ⚠ C# masks a shift count, it does not clamp it: `x << 32` on an `int` shifts by `32 & 31`, which is zero, so the expression is the identity rather than the zero almost everybody expects. On a `long` the mask is 63, so the same text is a genuine 32-bit shift. The rule therefore has to know the promoted width of the left operand and cannot be decided from syntax — a `byte` left operand promotes to `int` and masks with 31. There is no fix: rewriting `x << 33` to `x << 1` preserves the defect while making it look deliberate, and widening the operand guesses an intent the rule cannot read.

examples.bad: int mask = value << 32;
examples.good: long mask = (long)value << 32;

rules.falsePositives: Only built-in, non-lifted `<<`, `>>` and `>>>` whose result type is exactly `int`, `uint`, `long` or `ulong` are considered. ⚠ `nint` and `nuint` are excluded because their shift mask is 31 or 63 depending on the process, so the same source is correct on one platform and not the other and no single answer is right. A count already inside the width — including a literal `<< 0`, which is redundant but not masked — is not reported; only a count that the mask actually changes is. A constant zero left operand is reported separately as a result that is always zero, and only when the count is not itself constant, so that a fully constant expression the compiler already folded is not reported twice. Range-derived findings — a shift whose result is zero because the left operand's known values are too small — are outside this initial scope, and so are user-defined shift operators.

rules.title: The size comparison is decided by a count never being negative
rules.summary: A collection count or a length is compared against a constant that the count's own non-negativity already decides, so the comparison is always true or always false.
rules.rationale: `items.Count >= 0` is true for every value the framework can produce and `items.Count < 0` is true for none, so a guard written that way admits everything or nothing — and it is almost always a `> 0` that was typed wrong. ⚠ This is not SK2001. SK2001 folds a comparison the operand *type's* range decides, and a count is an `int`, whose range decides nothing at all about zero; the extra fact here is the framework contract that a count is never negative, which narrows the lower bound from `int.MinValue` to `0`. There is no fix, for the same reason SK2001 has none: the rule can prove the comparison is decided and cannot know whether the intended bound was `0` or `1`.

examples.bad: if (items.Count >= 0) { Process(items); }
examples.good: if (items.Count > 0) { Process(items); }

rules.falsePositives: The non-negative operand must be `Length` on an array, a `string`, a `Span`, a `ReadOnlySpan`, a `Memory` or a `ReadOnlyMemory`, `LongLength` on an array, a `Count` property whose declaring type implements `ICollection`, `ICollection<T>` or `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, or `Enumerable.Count`/`Enumerable.LongCount`. A `Count` on a type outside those contracts is not assumed to be non-negative. ⚠ A lifted comparison is excluded and that exclusion is load-bearing: `list?.Count >= 0` is `false` when `list` is null, so it is not always true and reporting it would be wrong. `IndexOf` and other members whose negative result is meaningful are not covered. Comparisons the operand type's range already decides are left to SK2001 rather than reported twice, and two constant operands are not reported at all.

rules.title: A signed modulus result is compared for equality with a non-zero value
rules.summary: A `%` on a possibly-negative signed operand is compared with `==` or `!=` against a non-zero constant, so the test fails for every value of the wrong sign.
rules.rationale: ⚠ C# gives `%` the sign of the dividend: `-5 % 2` is `-1`, not `1`. So `x % 2 == 1` is false for every negative odd `x`, and the parity check that reads as obviously correct is wrong on half its domain. ⚠ `x % 2 == 0` is **not** reported and must never be: zero has no sign, so comparing against it is correct for both signs — a rule that reported it would be wrong about the one spelling that is right. There is no fix, because the repair depends on what was meant: `!= 0` for a parity test, `Math.Abs(x % n) == k` for a magnitude test, and `x % n == k || x % n == -k` where both signs are wanted.

examples.bad: bool IsOdd(int value) => value % 2 == 1;
examples.good: bool IsOdd(int value) => value % 2 != 0;

rules.falsePositives: Reported only when the `%` result type is a signed fixed-width integral type, the comparison constant is not zero, and the dividend is not already proven non-negative. ⚠ The dividend is taken as non-negative when its own type is unsigned (`byte`, `ushort`, `uint`, `ulong`, `char` — so `someByte % 2 == 1` is correct and not reported even though the operation promotes to `int`), when it is a non-negative constant, when it is a collection count or a length, or when it is `Math.Abs`/`MathF.Abs`. Floating-point `%`, user-defined operators, lifted comparisons, native integers and `is` patterns over a modulus are outside this initial scope. Where a caller genuinely only ever passes non-negative values the finding is a true statement about the expression and a false alarm about the program; the repair is the same either way.

rules.title: The finalizer can throw
rules.summary: A `throw` can leave a finalizer, where nothing catches it and the process ends.
rules.rationale: An exception that escapes a finalizer is not caught anywhere. The runtime tears the process down from the finalizer thread, and the stack it prints names the finalizer queue rather than the code that put the object on it — so the one failure mode with no recovery path is also the one with the least diagnostic value. There is no `try` a caller can write that helps, because on that thread there is no caller.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The finalizer body is almost never where the throw is**, so the rule follows exactly one call hop, into a method declared on the same type whose body is in this compilation. The recall that costs is named rather than hidden: a `Dispose(bool)` inherited from another assembly is not followed, a throw two calls down is not followed, and a `virtual` member overridden by a derived type is read as the body the finalized type itself runs — which is why an `abstract` declaring type is skipped entirely. ⚠ **The `disposing` guard is what keeps the hop honest.** The disposal pattern's whole structure is `if (disposing) { ... }` holding the managed cleanup, which the finalizer path never enters; when the call site passes the literal `false`, throws that the branch condition proves unreachable are dropped, and without that every correct implementation of the pattern that throws anywhere in its managed half would be a false positive. Only an explicit `throw` counts — a finalizer that calls something which *might* throw is every finalizer ever written. A throw inside the `try` block of a `try`/`catch`, or inside a lambda or a local function, is not on the escaping path and is not reported. Report-only: wrapping the body in `catch { }` silences the rule and swallows the failure, deleting the `throw` deletes whatever the author meant by it, and which of the two is right is a decision about what the type owns.

rules.title: An exception is thrown from a `finally` block
rules.summary: A `throw` written inside a `finally` replaces whatever exception was already in flight.
rules.rationale: A `finally` runs while an exception is unwinding, and a `throw` from it does not join that exception — it replaces it. The failure that explains everything is destroyed, and the log is left holding the cleanup's complaint about a state the original failure created. The report names the one failure nobody can diagnose from, which is why this is worth a rule rather than a review comment.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Only an explicit `throw`.** A `finally` that calls a method which might throw is every `finally` ever written — `Dispose`, `Close` and `Flush` all can — so a rule asking "can anything in here throw" would fire across the whole tree and be switched off within a day. The keyword written inside the block is the author's own statement of intent and is the only thing the rule reads. A `throw` inside the `try` block of a nested `try`/`catch` within the `finally` never leaves it and is not reported, and neither is one held by a lambda or a local function, which may never be invoked. Nested `finally` blocks report against the innermost one that owns the keyword, so one `throw` produces one finding rather than one per enclosing clause. Report-only: deleting the `throw` discards whatever it was reporting and moving it out of the `finally` changes when it runs, and which of those the author meant is not visible in the block.

rules.title: `NullReferenceException` is caught
rules.summary: A `catch` clause names `NullReferenceException` as the type it handles.
rules.rationale: A `NullReferenceException` is a dereference that should not have happened, and naming it in a `catch` converts that bug into a control-flow path the program is expected to take. The handler also covers a region far larger than the one dereference that was meant, so the next null anywhere under the `try` is silently absorbed by a recovery written for a different one. The repair is a null check at the dereference, not a handler around the region.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **`catch (Exception)` catches it too and is deliberately not this rule.** A catch-all is a different decision with a different argument — sometimes a correct one at a process boundary — and folding the two together would make the finding unanswerable. The rule fires only where `NullReferenceException` is the type the clause itself names, which is the author stating that a null dereference is an expected outcome; a bare `catch`, a `catch (SystemException)` and a `catch (ArgumentNullException)` are all silent. ⚠ **Syntactic, matching the name as written**, in the three spellings a compiling program can use. The residual is a user-defined type whose own simple name is `NullReferenceException`, or a `using` alias for the framework one; neither occurs on either reference tree or anywhere in `Testing/corpus`, and buying them would cost the rule its ability to run under `--load=loose`, which is where most of the code an agent writes is first seen. Report-only: the repair is a null check somewhere under the `try` and not at the `catch`, no edit here can write it, and deleting the clause would turn a swallowed bug into a crash without anyone deciding that.

rules.title: The handler discards the exception it caught
rules.summary: The `catch` names the exception, throws a different one, and never passes the first to the second.
rules.rationale: `catch (SqlException error) { throw new ImportException("the import failed"); }` keeps the word "failed" and throws away the stack trace, the message, the error code and the cause. The caller is handed a sentence it cannot act on, and the frame that actually broke is no longer in the process. It looks like diligence, which is why it is more common than either the empty catch `SK2014` reports or the `throw ex;` restatement `SK2015` reports — and the repair is one argument.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Not `SK2014`.** That rule reports a `catch` whose block is *empty*, and its negative fixture asserts silence on any clause containing a statement; this one requires a statement, so the two cannot both fire on one clause. ⚠ **Disjoint from `SK7092` by construction rather than by filter.** `SK7092` requires the clause to propagate what it caught, by `throw;` or `throw error;`; this rule requires that it does **not**. The two conditions are negations of one another, so no clause can produce both findings and no `supersedes` entry is involved. ⚠ **The rule ships the half it can repair and names the half it omits.** A finding needs a `catch` that declared a variable — the author's own statement that the exception mattered — and a replacement type that already offers a constructor taking the same arguments plus a trailing `System.Exception`. Where no such constructor exists there is no edit to propose and the advice would be to redesign a type the handler's author may not own; where the clause binds no variable, `catch (FileNotFoundException) { throw new ConfigMissing(...); }` is a deliberate translation in which the type was the whole of the information. Passing the caught exception anywhere inside the construction — as the inner exception, or interpolated into the message — is silent, as is a `throw` inside a nested `try`/`catch`, a lambda or a local function. The fix appends the caught variable as the trailing argument and is `fixIsSafe: false`: it changes what a caller sees, and a boundary that deliberately hides the cause from an untrusted consumer is the one shape where the finding is right about the mechanism and wrong about the intent.

rules.title: `[ThreadStatic]` is applied where it cannot take effect
rules.resharperNote: The export carries two inspections for this concept — `ThreadStaticAtInstanceField` and `ThreadStaticFieldHasInitializer` — both at `warning`, and Skala reports them as one rule because they are one question asked of one declaration. `--resharper-severities` maps the first; the second has no separate Skala id and never will.
rules.summary: A field marked `[ThreadStatic]` is either not `static`, in which case the attribute does nothing at all, or is `static` with an initializer, in which case only the first thread to touch the type sees the initialized value.
rules.rationale: Thread-static storage is per-thread storage of a *static* slot. On an instance field there is already one slot per object and the runtime ignores the attribute entirely, so the isolation the author asked for was never there. ⚠ The initializer case is worse than nothing and is the one people actually hit: the initializer runs in the static constructor, once, on whichever thread reaches the type first. That thread sees the value and every other thread sees `default`. Nothing throws, nothing warns, and the field reads correctly in the debugger on the thread that happens to be attached — which is why the bug survives review and is found from a null reference on a background thread three weeks later.
rules.falsePositives: The attribute must resolve to `System.ThreadStaticAttribute` by namespace-qualified name, so a same-named attribute of the author's own is never touched. ⚠ **A `const` is excluded**: it is implicitly static and is required to carry an initializer, so neither half of the rule can be true of it and the repair the second half offers would not compile. ⚠ **`= 0`, `= false`, `= null` and `= default` are excluded**, and that is not tidiness — those initializers assign exactly what every thread but the first already sees, so there is no divergence between threads to report, and firing on them would make the rule fire on a declaration that is merely verbose. An instance field carrying an initializer is reported once, as an instance field: the initializer is beside the point when the attribute is inert to begin with, and two findings on one declaration would be the same defect counted twice. The non-static half reports once for the declaration because the modifier is shared by every declarator; the initializer half reports once per declarator, because `[ThreadStatic] static int a = 1, b;` is wrong about `a` and right about `b`. ⚠ **The fix for the non-static half deletes the attribute rather than inserting `static`, and the harness is what settled that.** Adding `static` turns an instance field with an initializer into a *static* field with an initializer, which is the other half of this same rule — so the fix fired the rule again on its own output and `skala fix` would have looped. Deleting the annotation makes the declaration say what it already does, in one edit, from any starting shape; the other repair moves where the value lives and which threads share it, which is why neither fix is marked safe. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: `[Pure]` is applied to a method that returns nothing
rules.summary: A `void` method carries `System.Diagnostics.Contracts.PureAttribute` or `JetBrains.Annotations.PureAttribute`, neither of which can be true of a method that returns nothing.
rules.rationale: The two accepted attributes fail for two different reasons and both fail. The BCL's `[Pure]` promises no visible state change; a `void` method that makes no visible state change and returns nothing has no observable effect at all, so either the annotation is wrong or the method is dead. JetBrains' `[Pure]` means the return value must be used; a `void` method has no return value, so the annotation is inapplicable by its own definition. ⚠ The annotation is load-bearing in Skala specifically: `SK2002` reads it to decide whether a discarded result matters, so an annotation that cannot be true feeds a second rule bad input.

examples.bad:
[Pure]
static void Validate(string input) => Check(input);
examples.good:
[Pure]
static bool IsValid(string input) => Check(input);

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **There are at least three different `PureAttribute`s and they do not mean the same thing**, so the rule resolves by namespace-qualified name and accepts exactly two: `System.Diagnostics.Contracts.PureAttribute` and `JetBrains.Annotations.PureAttribute`. Anything else spelled `PureAttribute` is declined — a third-party attribute that happens to share the simple name is under no obligation to mean either thing, and matching on the short name is how an annotation rule acquires false positives on code it has never seen. ⚠ **The comparison is a string rather than `Compilation.GetTypeByMetadataName`**, which returns null when two referenced assemblies both declare the name; JetBrains' annotations are routinely present twice, once from the package and once from a source-embedded `Annotations.cs`, and resolving by metadata name would silently answer "not that attribute" in exactly the repositories where the rule has the most to say. ⚠ **A method with an `out` or `ref` parameter is declined even when it returns `void`** — its results leave through the parameters, Code Contracts explicitly permitted that shape, and "returns nothing" is not true of it in the sense the rule means. Only methods and local functions are examined; `[Pure]` also targets a class, a property, an event, a parameter and a delegate, and on those there is no return type to contradict. One finding per declaration rather than one per annotation: two `[Pure]` attributes from two vendors on one `void` method is one mistake. ⚠ **The fix removes every accepted annotation, not only the one the finding points at** — a fix that left the second behind fired the rule again on its own output, which is a `skala fix` loop, and the harness caught that rather than the reasoning doing so. A list every one of whose attributes is being deleted goes as one span, because deleting them individually would leave `[]` behind and an empty attribute list does not parse. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: The `[DebuggerDisplay]` string names a member that does not exist
rules.summary: A `{…}` hole in a `[DebuggerDisplay]` string on a type declaration names a single identifier that is not a member of that type or of anything it inherits or implements.
rules.rationale: The expression is bound by the debugger at inspection time, not by the compiler, so a rename breaks it silently and it is discovered while debugging something else, at the moment it is least welcome. It is the same string-to-member binding `nameof` exists to remove, and the same class of defect as an `ArgumentException` naming a parameter that is not there. There is no fix: only the author knows which member was meant, and a rule that guessed would rename the display to whatever happened to be nearby.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The text inside the braces is a limited expression language, not a member name**, and a parser that guesses at it produces false positives on correct code. The accepted grammar is therefore deliberately tiny: one identifier, with an optional `this.` in front and an optional `,nq`-style all-letters format specifier behind. ⚠ **Anything else withdraws the whole attribute rather than the one hole** — a call, an index, an operator, a literal, a further `.`, a nested brace, an unbalanced brace, a comma this parser cannot account for. A string this parser only half understands is a string it has no standing to report on. ⚠ **The dotted path is the exclusion that matters most**: `{Owner.Name}` would need the member's type to answer and `{DateTime.Now}` has a root that is not a member of anything, so reporting either would be wrong for a different reason each time. ⚠ **The lookup searches implemented interfaces as well as base types, and a sabotage that failed to fail is what established that this is the guard doing the work.** The first version also matched a mangled explicit-implementation name — `ICollection.Count` ends with `.Count` — on the reasoning that a plain lookup misses an explicit implementation. The reasoning is true and the code was still redundant: an explicit implementation requires the interface to be in `AllInterfaces`, where the member is declared under its plain name, so the two guards covered exactly the same cases and *neither could be broken into failing*, each masking the other. The mangled match was removed as having no case of its own; the interface walk has one — **a default interface member**, which the type does not declare at all — and there is now a fixture that only it can save. **An error type anywhere on the base or interface chain withdraws the answer entirely** — an unresolved base reads as "no such member" and reporting it would be silently wrong, which is also why the rule finds nothing on a source slice with no dependency closure (#277). Only a class, struct, record or record struct declaration is examined; `[DebuggerDisplay]` also targets a field, a property and an assembly, and on those the expression binds against something other than the annotated declaration. The argument must be a compile-time constant string. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: The attribute is applied twice with the same arguments
rules.summary: One declaration carries the same `AllowMultiple` attribute more than once with provably identical arguments, so nothing distinguishes the second application from the first.
rules.rationale: ⚠ This is the one of issue #269's four sub-concepts the compiler is silent about, and the silence is the point. An attribute applied to a target it does not declare is `CS0592`; applied twice when `AllowMultiple` is false it is `CS0579`; naming a member that does not exist it is `CS8776` for the nullable-contract attributes and `SK2102` for `[DebuggerDisplay]`. For an `AllowMultiple` attribute the repetition is *legal* — it is simply indistinguishable from writing it once — so it survives review, and what it costs depends on who reads the metadata: a duplicated `[InlineData]` runs one test case twice under a name that says it ran once, and a duplicated `[SuppressMessage]` is dead metadata that the next person tries to work out the difference between.

examples.good:
[Conditional("TRACE")]
static void Log(string message) { }

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Identity is proved, never assumed.** If any argument on either application is not a compile-time constant or a `typeof`, the pair is declined: two expressions that might differ are not a repetition. Positional arguments are compared in order and named ones by name; a `name:` argument makes position and name two different orderings of one list and declines the pair rather than guessing. ⚠ **Only an attribute whose `AttributeUsage` reaches `AllowMultiple = true` is considered** — anything else cannot legally repeat, so a second application is `CS0579` and this rule has nothing to add to source that does not compile. The `AttributeUsage` lookup walks the attribute class's base chain, because that is what the runtime's own lookup does. ⚠ **`[method: X]` and `[return: X]` are two different things written on one declaration**, so the target is part of the group's identity and the two never compare against each other. ⚠ **Attribute lists on two `partial` declarations of one type are not compared**: the repetition is real but it is spread across files, the repair is a judgement about which file keeps it, and the answer would stop being decidable from the file the finding is in — which is what `scope: Semantic` promises the cache. Assembly-level lists are compared within one file for the same reason. The finding lands on the second and later applications, never the first, and the fix deletes that one application together with whichever separator it needs so the list still parses.

rules.title: The comparison is by reference where value equality was meant
rules.summary: `==` on a source class that defines value equality and declares no `operator ==`, so the comparison is by reference and cannot mean what it says.
rules.rationale: A type that overrides `Equals(object)` has written down what equality means for it, and `==` on that type does not use it: with no `operator ==` anywhere on the chain the comparison falls back to reference identity, so two instances the type itself calls equal compare `false`. It does not fail, which is why it survives review and outlives the test suite.

examples.bad:
// Money overrides Equals(object) and declares no operator ==
if (left == right) { }
examples.good: if (Equals(left, right)) { }

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Only the built-in reference `==` is reported.** An operation that binds to a user-defined operator is never a finding, which excludes records, `string`, `Uri`, `Version` and every type that declares `operator ==` on itself or inherits one from a base — the check is on the bound operator, not on a list of names. Both operands must have the *same* named type, and that type must be a class **declared in this compilation**: a framework type whose `Equals` override the author cannot see is deliberately out of scope, because `encoding == Encoding.UTF8` reads as identity against a cached singleton and calling it wrong needs knowledge of what the library guarantees. `null` and `default` operands are never reported, because a null check is not a value comparison; neither is an operand spelled `this` or `base`. Nothing inside `Equals`, `GetHashCode`, `CompareTo` or `operator ==`/`!=` is reported at all — an identity short circuit there is the idiom rather than a mistake. Interfaces, type parameters, delegates, `object` and error types are excluded. ⚠ **`ReferenceEquals` on a value type is not part of this rule, and it was built before it was withdrawn.** A probe compiled against a real project showed `CA2013` reporting exactly that shape, with the same advice, enabled by default — so ADR-008 hosts it rather than Skala restating it, and `ReferenceEqualsWithValueType` is recorded in the hosted map instead of the parity map. ⚠ **Two more inspections in this concept are declined.** `CompareNonConstrainedGenericWithNull` (`t == null` on an unconstrained `T`) is declined because the repair is a constraint or an `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` call rather than an edit to the comparison, and because the export itself ships it at `none`; `CheckForReferenceEqualityInstead` is the mirror direction and asks what the author meant rather than what the code does, which is not decidable from the shape. The fix rewrites the comparison to `Equals(a, b)`, which is null-safe and dispatches to the override; it carries `fixIsSafe: false` because it changes the answer, and changing the answer is the entire point of the finding. ⚠ **A type whose base list did not bind is withdrawn, and that was found by measuring rather than by reading.** On the reference trees a class declaring `IEquatable<Self>` was reported for not implementing it: without the SDK's implicit global usings the name bound to an *error* type, so the interface list held `IEquatable<>` and the comparison against `System.IEquatable`1` failed. Skala loads a compilation three ways and two of them can be incomplete, so an error type among a type's bases or interfaces now withdraws it from every rule in this batch — the same discipline `SK7080` uses for an inheritance chain it cannot walk.

rules.title: `base.Equals` or `base.GetHashCode` resolves to `object`'s
rules.summary: An equality member calls `base.Equals` or `base.GetHashCode` where the base is `System.Object`, so the delegation it was written to perform returns reference identity and the identity hash.
rules.rationale: The override exists to replace identity with value semantics, and `base` is identity — the one thing it was written to stop doing. `base.GetHashCode()` inside `GetHashCode` returns the runtime's per-instance number, so two equal objects hash differently and the type is unusable as a dictionary key however carefully `Equals` was written. `base.Equals(other)` inside `Equals` returns reference equality, so the override answers the question it was overriding. It is a copy-paste result and a generated-stub result, and it reads as diligence.
rules.falsePositives: The receiver must be spelled `base`, the call must sit inside an equality member of the declaring type — `Equals`, `GetHashCode` or `CompareTo` — and the call must **bind** to a member of `System.Object`. An intermediate base class that overrides equality is doing real work, and delegating to it is correct and is never reported. `base.GetHashCode()` in a struct binds to `ValueType.GetHashCode`, which does hash the fields, and is likewise not reported. ⚠ **Fixless, and the reason is that both repairs are edits somebody has to choose between.** Deleting the call changes what the member returns, and replacing it needs to know which fields identity is made of — the one thing the analysis cannot recover from a body that never mentions them. A generated `HashCode.Combine(...)` over every field would be a guess presented as a repair, which is worse than no fix in exactly the situation where the author was already not paying attention.

rules.title: The hash code reads state that equality ignores
rules.summary: `GetHashCode` reads an instance member that none of the type's `Equals` methods compares, so two instances the type calls equal can hash differently.
rules.rationale: The hash code contract runs in one direction only: equal objects must hash the same. A hash computed over a member that equality ignores breaks it head-on — two objects differing only in that member are equal and land in different buckets, so the second one inserted into a dictionary hides neither and finds neither, `Remove` returns `false` while `Count` still counts it, and a freshly built key never matches the entry it names. ⚠ **The reverse direction is not a defect and is deliberately not reported.** An `Equals` that compares more members than the hash reads only makes the hash weaker: every equal pair still hashes the same, which is all the contract asks. That direction is a collision-quality observation, and shipping it as a correctness finding would be one more rule that is usually right.
rules.falsePositives: The type must declare both `GetHashCode()` and at least one `Equals`, all of them with bodies in the one file that declares the type, and must not be a record — a partial type withdraws rather than being examined from one half. ⚠ **An equality set that comes back empty withdraws the type**: an `Equals` that reads no member of its own type is comparing identity, returning a constant or delegating to `base`, and treating "compares nothing" as the equality set would turn every hashed member into a finding. ⚠ **A call, in either body, to a method this type declares that is not one of its own equality members withdraws the type entirely.** A helper the analysis cannot read produces an *under*-counted equality set, and an under-counted equality set is precisely what reports a member the type does compare — the one wrong answer this rule must not give. Local functions and lambdas inside the bodies are read, because they are in the body. A property and the single field its getter returns are one piece of state, and so are an auto-property and its backing field; without that the rule would report every hand-written property in the repository. `nameof(x)` names a member and reads nothing, so it is not a read. One finding per member, reported on the member's mention in the hash. ⚠ **Mutability is not this rule's question**: a hashed member that equality *does* compare is `SK2043`'s finding, and the two partition the hashed members between them by construction rather than by filtering each other's output. Fixless — dropping the member from the hash and adding it to `Equals` are both one edit, they are opposite decisions about what the type means, and no signal in the code says which was intended. ⚠ **A type whose base list did not bind is withdrawn, and that was found by measuring rather than by reading.** On the reference trees a class declaring `IEquatable<Self>` was reported for not implementing it: without the SDK's implicit global usings the name bound to an *error* type, so the interface list held `IEquatable<>` and the comparison against `System.IEquatable`1` failed. Skala loads a compilation three ways and two of them can be incomplete, so an error type among a type's bases or interfaces now withdraws it from every rule in this batch — the same discipline `SK7080` uses for an inheritance chain it cannot walk.

rules.title: The hash code depends on state that can change
rules.summary: `GetHashCode` on a class reads an equality-relevant instance member that can still be assigned after construction.
rules.rationale: An object whose hash changes after it was stored is lost inside its own dictionary. The bucket was chosen with the old hash and every lookup computes the new one, so the entry is present and unreachable: `Remove` returns `false`, `Count` still counts it, `ContainsKey` says no and enumeration says yes. Nothing throws and nothing logs, and the report that comes back is that an item "disappeared" — which sends the reader to the collection rather than to the key.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Classes only.** A struct is copied into the collection, so mutating the original cannot move the stored copy; the hazard this rule names needs reference identity to exist at all, and reporting it on structs would be reporting a different, much weaker thing under the same message. ⚠ **A private field that nothing assigns outside a constructor is not reported, even though it is not marked `readonly`.** That is the largest false-positive class in this shape and it is decidable rather than guessed: a private member can only be assigned inside the type's own declaration, so the assignments — including `++`, compound assignment and `ref`/`out` arguments — can be counted. Only a type declared in one file is examined, because that count is only complete for one. `readonly` fields, `const`s, statics, getter-only auto-properties and `init`-only auto-properties are never reported: none of them can change after the object exists. A property whose setter is not private is reported without the assignment scan, because any assembly can call it. ⚠ **The member must also be one the type's equality compares**, and that is what keeps this rule and `SK2042` from arguing over one span: a member the hash reads is either compared by `Equals`, and then mutability is the open question and it is asked here, or it is not compared, and then the finding is `SK2042`'s. The partition is total and neither rule filters the other. A type that declares no `Equals` at all, or whose equality set could not be read, has every hashed member examined here and nothing reported by `SK2042`. Fixless — `readonly` is not an available repair, because the rule only fires where something does assign the member; whether to freeze the state, drop the member from the hash, or stop using the type as a key is a design decision with three different blast radii. ⚠ **A type whose base list did not bind is withdrawn, and that was found by measuring rather than by reading.** On the reference trees a class declaring `IEquatable<Self>` was reported for not implementing it: without the SDK's implicit global usings the name bound to an *error* type, so the interface list held `IEquatable<>` and the comparison against `System.IEquatable`1` failed. Skala loads a compilation three ways and two of them can be incomplete, so an error type among a type's bases or interfaces now withdraws it from every rule in this batch — the same discipline `SK7080` uses for an inheritance chain it cannot walk.

rules.title: The equality members are inconsistent with each other
rules.summary: A type declares one half of an equality or ordering contract and not the other: `Equals(Self)` with no `IEquatable<Self>`, or `==` and `IComparable` with no relational operators.
rules.rationale: Each is one decision written down once and not the second time, and each leaves two spellings of the same question giving different answers. A typed `Equals(Self)` that no interface advertises is invisible to `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`, to `Dictionary<Self, …>` and to every `where T : IEquatable<T>` constraint, so the type is compared through the object overload it was written to avoid — boxing on a struct, and identity on a class that has no override. A type that defines `==` and also orders itself, without `<` and `>`, offers half an operator set and sends the reader to `CompareTo` to find out whether the other half exists.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **One finding per type, in a fixed order, never one per sub-case.** The two are aspects of a single omission, and reporting them separately would multiply one decision by how many ways it shows. ⚠ **`SK2004`'s span is left to `SK2004`**: a type implementing `IEquatable<Self>` with no `Equals(object)` override is that rule's finding, and this one asks its precondition first and stays silent where it holds — by construction, not by a severity filter, so neither rule can be turned on into a duplicate. The typed `Equals` must take exactly the declaring type and return `bool`, so `Equals(string)` on something that is not a string is an overload rather than a contract; an explicit interface implementation counts as implementing the interface. Records are excluded, because the compiler writes all of it. The ordering half fires only on a type that already declares `==`, which is what separates a type in the operator business from the many that implement `IComparable<T>` so a `Sort` call works and want no operators at all; `CA1036` covers the same ground and was measured *not* to fire at the SDK's recommended analysis level, which is why this half stands. ⚠ **`S3875`'s core — `operator ==` with no `Equals(object)` override — was built and then withdrawn.** A probe compiled against a real project reports it as `CS0660` and `CS0661`: compiler warnings, always on, needing no analyzer package and no configuration. Restating a diagnostic the compiler already emits is the double-count doc 17 excludes on sight, and it would have shipped had the probe not been compiled. ⚠ **`S4035` — "classes implementing `IEquatable<T>` should be sealed" — is declined rather than implemented.** Unsealed is not the defect; the defect is an `Equals` that accepts a derived instance through an `is T` test, so that a base and a derived instance compare equal in one direction and not the other. That is a different analysis with a different false-positive story, it needs its own id and its own measurement, and a shape-only finding on every unsealed `IEquatable<T>` would report the many that handle it correctly. Fixless — adding `IEquatable<Self>` to a base list changes a public surface, and an operator set cannot be generated from an ordering. Each is a review, not a text edit. ⚠ **A type whose base list did not bind is withdrawn, and that was found by measuring rather than by reading.** On the reference trees a class declaring `IEquatable<Self>` was reported for not implementing it: without the SDK's implicit global usings the name bound to an *error* type, so the interface list held `IEquatable<>` and the comparison against `System.IEquatable`1` failed. Skala loads a compilation three ways and two of them can be incomplete, so an error type among a type's bases or interfaces now withdraws it from every rule in this batch — the same discipline `SK7080` uses for an inheritance chain it cannot walk.

rules.title: The condition is an assignment, not a comparison
rules.summary: The whole condition of an `if`, `while`, `do` or `for` is a simple assignment, so the condition stores a value and then tests what it stored rather than comparing anything.
rules.rationale: `if (x = y)` compiles only where the assigned type is `bool`, which is exactly why the mistake survives the compiler and why the rule can exist at all. The branch then runs whenever `y` is true, and the value the author meant to compare against is silently overwritten. ⚠ **The signal is that the assignment is the *entire* condition.** `while ((line = reader.ReadLine()) != null)` assigns inside a condition too, and is correct and common; there the assignment is an operand of a comparison, not the condition itself. Wrapping the assignment in its own parentheses — `if ((ok = TryLoad()))` — is the convention C programmers have used for forty years to say the assignment was meant, and the rule honours it.

examples.bad: if (ready = pending) { Start(); }

rules.falsePositives: Only a simple `=` is examined, and only where it is the complete condition of an `if`, `while`, `do` or `for`. ⚠ **An assignment nested inside the condition is never reported** — `while ((line = reader.ReadLine()) != null)`, `if ((node = node.Parent) is not null)` and `if (Init() && (handle = Open()) != Invalid)` are the read-assign-test idiom and are correct; the assignment there is an operand, not the condition. ⚠ **An extra pair of parentheses withdraws the finding**: `if ((ok = TryLoad()))` is the long-standing convention for saying the assignment is deliberate, and a rule that ignored it would leave no way to write the intended code. Compound assignments — `flag |= Check()`, `count += 1` — are a different shape with a different repair and are not reported. A `for` statement's initialiser and incrementor are not conditions and are not examined. ⚠ **A `?:` condition is not examined, and the reason is the grammar rather than a judgement**: assignment binds looser than `?:`, so `x = flag = other ? 1 : 2` parses as `x = (flag = (other ? 1 : 2))` and a bare assignment can never be a ternary condition. Writing one requires the parentheses this rule already exempts, so the first draft's `ConditionalExpression` registration was a guard that could not fire. There is no fix, because the repair is a choice the rule cannot make: `==` and a parenthesised assignment are both plausible and they are different programs. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: Both operands of the operator are the same expression
rules.summary: Both operands of `&&`, `||`, `&`, `|`, `^`, `-`, `/` or `%` are the same side-effect-free expression, so the operator answers a question about nothing.
rules.rationale: `a && a`, `offset - offset`, `bits ^ bits` — one side was meant to name something else and a copy-paste left it naming the first. The result is a constant the compiler is happy to fold, and the check that was written to catch a case cannot catch it. ⚠ **The six comparison operators are not examined, and measuring rather than remembering is what settled that.** `csc` reports `q == q`, `q < q`, `this.g == this.g`, `b.v == b.v`, `Box.Which == Box.Which` and `a == a` on a string as `CS1718`, on by default; the only comparison shape it leaves silent is a property access, and `SK2012` already owns that. There was nothing left over, so the operators went. ⚠ **The rule must still know the operand's type, which is why it is semantic.** `x - x` on a `double` is a NaN-preserving zero, not a constant nothing.

examples.bad: if (options.verbose || options.verbose) { Trace(); }

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The six comparison operators are not examined at all**, because `csc` already reports every shape this rule could have reported: `CS1718` covers simple names, `this.` paths, member access to a field, static fields, strings and reference equality, and it is on by default.
