The one comparison shape the compiler leaves silent is a property access, and `SK2012` already covers that with a proof about the accessor bodies this rule does not have. ⚠ **Doc 08's sentence that `CS1717`/`CS1718` "reach the identifier spellings only" is wrong and was refuted by this measurement** — it is true of properties, which is the example it was written from, and false of fields reached through a member access. ⚠ **Floating-point operands are excluded outright.** `x - x` on a `double` is 0 for every finite value and NaN for NaN and the infinities, which is a real technique for propagating NaN and is textually identical to the defect; `double`, `float`, `decimal` and their nullable forms never reach the report. ⚠ **Only side-effect-free paths of locals, parameters, fields, `this` and `base` are compared.** An invocation on either side is two evaluations that may differ — `reader.Read() - reader.Read()` is not a defect — and a property access is a method call whose two evaluations the rule does not attempt to prove equal. ⚠ **`Math.Max(x, x)` and `a.CompareTo(a)` are invocations, not operators, and are outside the subject entirely**; a generator emitting them is not reported. A user-defined operator, a lifted (nullable-operand) operation and an operand of an unresolved type are all excluded, because none of them has the meaning the rule assumes. `+`, `*`, `<<` and `>>` are not examined: doubling, squaring and shifting by oneself are ordinary arithmetic. `=` is not examined either — the compiler's own `CS1717` says it, and `SK2012` says the rest. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: A later condition in the chain repeats an earlier one
rules.summary: One `if`/`else if` chain tests the same side-effect-free condition twice, so the later branch is unreachable and the case it was written for is never handled.
rules.rationale: In an `if`/`else if` chain nothing at all runs between one condition and the next: reaching the second means the first was false, so a second condition identical to the first is false too and its body is dead. No compiler reports it, because the code is perfectly well formed — it simply does something other than what it looks like. ⚠ **The comparison is structural, not textual.** `if (a && b)` and `if (b && a)` are different conditions and neither is reported for the other; two conditions that merely share a sub-expression — `if (x.Kind == A) … else if (x.Kind == B)` — are different conditions too. Only a whole condition equal to a whole earlier condition, token for token and ignoring layout, is a finding.

examples.bad: if (mode == Mode.Fast) { Fast(); } else if (mode == Mode.Fast) { Careful(); }
examples.good: if (mode == Mode.Fast) { Fast(); } else if (mode == Mode.Careful) { Careful(); }

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Sequential `if` statements are deliberately not reported, and that is the rule's main exclusion.** Two separate `if`s testing the same thing are only pointless when nothing between them changed the answer, and the first body usually did exactly that — `if (dirty) { Flush(); } if (dirty) { … }` needs the bodies read before it means anything. Only conditions inside one `if`/`else if` chain, where no statement can run between the two tests, are compared. ⚠ **The condition must be side-effect free**: an invocation, an `await`, an assignment, an `++` or a `--` anywhere in either condition withdraws the finding, because `if (Read()) … else if (Read())` really is two different questions. ⚠ **Structural equality, never text.** `SyntaxFactory.AreEquivalent` compares the trees ignoring trivia, so layout, line breaks and comments do not decide it, and neither does a shared sub-expression: only complete conditions are compared with each other, never their parts. Element access is excluded because an indexer is a call. A condition containing a preprocessor directive is excluded, because the two branches of an `#if` are not the same program. ⚠ **The side-effect test is asked once, of the later condition, and once is enough**: `IsRepeatable` is a pure function of the syntax and the structural comparison compares the syntax, so two equal conditions always answer it the same way. A second copy of the guard was in the first draft and a sabotage proved no test could reach it. Every later condition is compared against every earlier one in its own chain and the finding points at the repeat, not at the original. There is no fix: which of the two conditions was meant to be something else, and what, is the entire content of the bug. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: The operator sequence reads as a different operator
rules.summary: An `=` is written hard against a following unary `-`, `+` or `!` and separated from the operand — `x =- 1` — so the pair reads as the compound operator `-=` and is not one.
rules.rationale: `x =- 1` assigns negative one. `x -= 1` subtracts one. C# has no `=-` operator, so the compiler splits the two characters silently and the reader's eye does not. ⚠ **The whitespace is the entire signal, and it is the only signal there is.** `x = -1` and `x =- 1` are the same program and differ only in layout, so nothing semantic can separate the deliberate from the mistyped; what separates them is that somebody wrote the `=` and the sign as one token and then put a space before the number, which is how `-=` is spelled and not how a negative literal is. A rule that ignored trivia here would have nothing left to look at.

examples.bad: remaining =- 1;

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Two conditions must hold together, and each one alone would over-fire.** The `=` and the unary operator must be adjacent with no trivia between them, and the unary operator must be separated from its operand by trivia. `x = -1` and `x = - 1` fail the first; `x =-1` and `x=-1` fail the second, and they are how a negative literal gets written in a hurry and in a compressed style. Only the asymmetric spelling — where the spacing groups the two operator characters together and pushes the operand away — is reported, whether or not there is a space before the `=`. ⚠ **A third condition, "there is space before the `=`", was in the first draft and was removed because a sabotage could not reach it**: no fixture separated it from the other two, and `x=- 1` groups and pushes exactly as `x =- 1` does, so declining it was an exemption with no argument behind it. ⚠ **The rule reads the trivia of the tree as parsed**, which is the source as the author wrote it; it draws no conclusion from what the formatter would produce, and running the formatter over the file is one of the ways to make the finding go away. Only `-`, `+` and `!` are considered: they are the unary operators whose characters also start a compound assignment (`-=`, `+=`, `!=`). A `~` or a `&` has no such reading. Compound assignments themselves are not examined, and neither is any binary operator, and neither is a variable declarator's `=`, which is not an assignment expression. ⚠ There is **no fix**, deliberately: `x -= 1` and `x = -1` are both plausible readings and they are different programs, so an automatic repair would have to guess which bug it was looking at. ⚠ **Measured on the 4 459-file corpus, and the second condition is what earned its place there.** The shipped rule reports nothing. Widened to look only at the `=`/sign adjacency, it reports **17** occurrences, every one of them inside `Testing/corpus/unformatted/collapse/` — a slice whose whole purpose is to strip whitespace, so `GoalIndex = -1;` is stored as `GoalIndex=-1;`. The operand is not pushed away from the sign in any of them, which is why the rule declines all 17. A tool that reads whitespace for meaning meets machine-mangled whitespace sooner than most, and this is what that looks like. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: Use && or || rather than & or | on booleans
rules.summary: A `&` or `|` joins two `bool` operands whose right side has no side effect, so the non-short-circuiting operator evaluates a guard's right half that the guard exists to skip.
rules.rationale: `if (node != null & node.Ready)` evaluates `node.Ready` whichever way the null check went, so the check protects nothing and the `NullReferenceException` it was written to prevent is thrown anyway. One character separates it from the code that works. ⚠ **The rule is semantic because the operand type decides everything.** `&` and `|` on integers and on `[Flags]` enums are the *only* way to write those operations, and reporting `flags & Mask` would be a catastrophe rather than a false positive; the rule therefore fires only where both operands are non-nullable `bool` and the operator is the language's own, never a user-defined one.

examples.bad: if (node != null & node.Ready) { Use(node); }

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Integral and enum operands are excluded, and nothing else in this rule matters as much.** `flags & Mask`, `a | b` on `int`, and every `[Flags]` combination are `&`/`|` used correctly and have no `&&` form at all; the rule reads the operand types and fires only where both are exactly non-nullable `System.Boolean`. ⚠ **`bool?` is excluded too, and it is not the same exclusion.** Lifted `&` and `|` on nullable booleans are three-valued — `null & false` is `false`, not `null` — and `&&`/`||` cannot express that, so the rewrite would change the answer rather than the evaluation order. A user-defined `operator &` or `operator |`, and any operand whose type did not resolve, are excluded for the same reason: the operator does not mean what the rule assumes. ⚠ **A right operand with a side effect is deliberate and is never reported.** An invocation, an assignment, an `await`, an `++`, an object creation or an element access on the right is the documented reason to reach for `&` — both validators must run so both messages are collected — and short-circuiting it would delete work. Only a right operand built from names, member-access paths, literals, `is`/`as` tests and comparisons over them is reported. ⚠ **A mixed bitwise expression is declined rather than reported**, because `&` and `|` bind tighter than `&&` and `||` and swapping one token inside `a | b & c` regroups the whole expression. If the node's parent, or either of its operands, is another `&`, `|` or `^`, the rule stays silent — an under-report in the one place where the fix could silently change the program. `^` is not examined at all: it has no short-circuiting form. The fix replaces the single operator token and nothing else, so it is safe to apply without review. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: The method ignores its inputs and returns a constant
rules.summary: A `private` method takes parameters, reads none of them, and returns a compile-time constant — the shape a placeholder body has when the signature was written before the logic.
rules.rationale: This is the failure that compiles. A method with the right name, the right parameters and the right return type, whose body is `return 0;`, satisfies every caller, passes a smoke test, and is wrong — and it is exactly what gets written when the shape of the work is known and the work is not. On AI-written code it is the single most common way a stub survives review: nothing about it looks unfinished, because a `TODO` was never written and a `NotImplementedException` was never thrown. The parameters are the tell. Computing an argument and handing it to a method that cannot read it is work the program does for no reason, and it is visible in the declaration.
rules.falsePositives:
⚠ **The legitimate forms of "returns a constant" outnumber the defective ones, and `private` is what separates them — not a conservative default that gets widened later.** An interface implementation, a `virtual` hook meant to be overridden, a test double, a `NotImplementedException` stub and a strategy that genuinely is constant are all methods whose body is a constant on purpose, and every one of them is reached from outside the type. A `private` method is the only case where the rule can see every caller, and therefore the only case where "the parameters are computed and thrown away" is a statement about the program rather than about one declaration.

⚠ **The recall cost is the entire public and internal surface, which is where an AI-written stub is most likely to be.** That is stated rather than hidden: doc 08's bar is zero false positives, and there is no predicate over a visible method that separates a placeholder from a deliberate constant. `abstract`, `virtual`, `override`, `new`, `partial`, `extern` and `async` are excluded for the same reason, as is any method carrying an attribute — `[Conditional]`, a generator's marker, a serializer's hook are all reasons the body is what it is that the rule cannot read.

⚠ **A method group withdraws the finding.** `private static bool Always(Item i) => true;` passed to `Where` is a predicate whose whole point is that it ignores its input, and nothing but its use separates it from a stub. The reference scan is `SK4021`'s and is sound for the same reason: the containing type is required to have a single declaration, so every reference to a private member is in that one file. `nameof(Method)` reaches the scan as a non-invocation reference and withdraws the finding too — conservatively, because a name written down is a use the rule cannot follow.

**One `return`, not "every `return` is the same constant".** A method with two returns has a branch, and a branch reads something — if not a parameter then state — and either way it is not the placeholder this rule is about. `nameof(parameter)` is excluded explicitly: it is a constant that reads its input, and it is the one way both halves of the predicate can hold while the finding is wrong. A parameterless method returning a constant is a named constant and is never reported.

⚠ **No fix, and the reason is that there is no edit.** What the method should return is the logic that was never written; deleting the method breaks its callers, and throwing `NotImplementedException` trades a silent wrong answer for a crash without deciding anything. The finding is the whole contribution.

rules.title: The base type tests `this` against a derived type
rules.summary: A class asks whether `this` is one of its own subclasses, so adding a subclass means editing the base and nothing tells anyone when a case is missing.
rules.rationale: The dependency runs the wrong way. A base type is supposed to be the thing subclasses know about, and here it is the thing that knows about them: adding a subclass means opening the base and finding every `is` that has to learn about it. It is polymorphism written as a chain of `if`s, with none of the checking that makes an `abstract` member work — a missing `override` is a compile error, and a missing branch is a wrong answer at run time that nothing anywhere reports. The repair is nearly always a member on the base that each subclass overrides, which moves the decision to where the compiler can see it.
rules.falsePositives:
⚠ **The same shape is how a closed hierarchy dispatches, and that form is declined rather than reported.** A base whose instance constructors are all `private` cannot be derived from outside its own declaration, so its subclasses are exactly the ones written inside it, the set is fixed at compile time, and a test over them cannot silently miss a case. That is a discriminated union emulated in C#, not a missing `virtual`, and the compiler is enforcing the exhaustiveness this rule otherwise exists to say nobody is enforcing.

⚠ **That guard is a sufficient condition for the legitimate form and not a necessary one, which is why the rule ships at `suggestion` rather than the `warning` the proposal asked for.** A hierarchy closed by convention — every subclass `sealed`, all of them in one file, a `protected` constructor and a code review that would catch a new one — is indistinguishable here from an open one, and it is still reported. The finding is a question worth asking, not a defect the tool can prove.

**The tested type must derive from the type of `this`, and one base-type walk decides that and four other things.** `this is ISomething` is a capability probe rather than a question about the hierarchy; a struct cannot be derived from; `this is Base` — the containing type itself — is always true and is a different finding; a `sealed` type has no subclasses; and a subclass outside this compilation would be a hierarchy whose other half the rule has never read. ⚠ **All five were written as separate guards first, and a sabotage pass proved that none of them can fail.** The walk starts one link above the tested type and only ever visits classes, which answers every one of them, so they are recorded in the analyzer rather than kept as checks no fixture could exercise. The last is the one worth naming: a type in metadata cannot derive from a type in the compilation that references it, and `this` only exists in source, so "declared in this compilation" is not a condition that can be false.

**Only `this` written out.** A local holding the same instance is an ordinary type test on an ordinary value — a visitor, an equality check, a dispatcher. What makes this a design finding is that the type is asking about *itself*, and that is a syntactic property.

**Both the operator and the pattern forms are matched**: `this is Derived`, `this is Derived d`, `this is Derived { Property: 1 }`. ⚠ A `switch` over `this` is not, and that is a stated gap rather than a decision: it is the same defect written differently, and the fixture set for it has not been built.

⚠ **No fix.** The repair is a virtual member on the base and an `override` on each subclass — several edits across several files, and the choice of what the member should be called and what it should return is the design decision the rule is asking the author to make. An edit that could write it would be an edit that already knew the answer.

rules.title: Null is returned where an empty sequence was expected
rules.summary: A method whose return type is an array or a sequence interface returns `null`, so every caller has to null-check before iterating and the ones that forget fail at a `foreach`.
rules.rationale: A sequence return type is a promise that the result can be iterated, and `null` breaks it in the one way the type system does not catch. The failure lands at a `foreach` in the caller, not at the `return` that caused it, and the stack names the wrong file. The cost of keeping the promise is nothing: `[]` for a `T[]` is `Array.Empty<T>()`, which is a singleton, and for a `List<T>` it is one empty list against one null check in every caller for ever. "Empty" and "absent" are also not usually different questions for a sequence — a caller that needs to tell them apart is asking about something other than the elements, and a nullable return type is how to say so.
rules.falsePositives:
⚠ **An `IEnumerable<T>?` return type is declined, and that is the intended way to disagree with the rule.** The annotation is the author saying null is a value this method returns; the contract already carries the warning that an unguarded `foreach` would be wrong, and the rule has nothing to add to a decision made on purpose. The check reads the symbol's nullable annotation rather than the syntax, because in the `async` case the annotation sits on the type argument inside the task and there is no `?` on the declaration to look at.

⚠ **Disjoint from `SK3020` by construction, and the `async` half is the reason to say so.** `SK3020` reports a non-`async` method whose declared return type is `Task` returning null — a null *task*, which throws at the `await`. This rule requires the *effective* return type to be a sequence. For a non-`async` `Task<IEnumerable<T>>` the declared type is a task, so this rule declines and `SK3020` reports; for the `async` form `SK3020` declines by its own `async` guard and this rule reports the null sequence inside a real task. The two predicates cannot both hold, so neither declares `supersedes` — which dedupes on a shared span and would suppress one of two findings rather than leaving each a property of its own rule. A fixture asserts both directions.

**The type is matched by declaration, never by assignability, and the list is exactly what `[]` constructs**: any array, `IEnumerable<T>`, `ICollection<T>`, `IList<T>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, `IReadOnlyList<T>`, `List<T>`. `string` is an `IEnumerable<char>` and is not a sequence in the sense meant here; `IDictionary<K, V>` is deliberately absent because a collection expression does not target-type to it, and a fix that did not compile would be worse than a finding never made. ⚠ **The cost is that a `Dictionary<K, V>` returning null is not reported**, which is a stated gap rather than a judgement that it is fine.

**Methods and local functions only.** A property or an indexer returning a null sequence is the same defect and is not reported; the shape has more forms — an arrow body, a `get` accessor, an auto-property's backing store — and the fixture set for them has not been built. It is a gap, not a decision.

⚠ **The fix is `[]` and the rule is silent below C# 12**, rather than offering an edit that does not compile: `hasFix: true` is a promise about every finding, not most of them. `fixIsSafe: false` because a caller that already tests the result for null keeps compiling and stops taking a branch it was written to take — the edit is right and the review is about whether that branch mattered.

rules.title: The method name does not reflect its synchronicity
rules.summary: A method returning an awaitable is not named `…Async`, or a method named `…Async` returns nothing to await. Ships disabled; turn it on per path where the convention is adopted.
rules.rationale: The `Async` suffix is how a caller knows a result must be awaited, and it is what makes a missing `await` visible in review rather than at run time — the fire-and-forget shape `SK3005` reports. Read the other way it matters as much: a name ending in `Async` on a method that returns nothing to await tells every caller to write an `await` that will not compile, or worse, to assume work is happening in the background that is not.

examples.bad: public Task<Order> Load(int id) => store.FindAsync(id);
examples.good: public Task<Order> LoadAsync(int id) => store.FindAsync(id);

rules.falsePositives:
⚠ **This is a naming convention, which is the most opinionated thing a linter can hold an opinion about, and it ships `defaultSeverity: none` — but the measurement that decided it is not the one that was expected.** Run over Skala's own solution from a fresh Release binlog, with the severity temporarily raised and every exclusion below in force, the rule reports **1** finding: a `private static async Task<List<JsonObject>> Converse(…)` test helper in `Rikarin.Skala.Server.Tests`, which is a correct finding. Zero in the reverse direction. ⚠ **The number that matters is the second one: the whole population this rule governs in Skala's first-party source is 5 methods.** Widening the rule to report every asynchronous method regardless of its name — the count a repository that had not adopted the convention would see — returns 5, of which 4 already carry the suffix.

**A population of five cannot calibrate a naming convention, and that is the argument for `none`.** A low count on Skala's own tree is not evidence the rule is quiet; it is evidence that Skala already writes the suffix, and doc 08's standing warning is that a reference tree is a test subject and never a specification. Nothing available measures a repository that has *not* adopted the convention, and shipping at `suggestion` would be Skala asserting a naming policy on evidence it does not have. It is opt-in exactly the way `SK7010` and `SK7101` are: a repository that has adopted the convention turns it on per path and gets it enforced, and one that has not is not told its whole codebase is wrong.

⚠ **The same run refuted a first measurement of 10, which came from a broken loader.** `--load=workspace` on this tree produces 4 375 CS errors; under it `Xunit.FactAttribute` does not resolve, the test-method exclusion below silently does nothing, and eight test methods are reported that the sound run correctly declines. A zero — or a ten — from a compilation that did not bind is not a measurement.

⚠ **The exclusions are not edge cases; on a real tree they are most of the suffix-less `Task`-returning methods.** An `override` and an interface implementation — explicit or implicit — take their name from the declaration they satisfy, so the finding would be made in a file the author cannot fix. An ASP.NET MVC action, a Razor page handler and a SignalR hub method are named by a routing convention that adding the suffix would break; the containing type's base chain, `[ApiController]` and any attribute deriving from `HttpMethodAttribute` are all read. A test method is named after what it asserts, and a suite that renamed every one of them would be worse to read; xUnit, NUnit and MSTest attributes are all recognised, and so are their lifecycle hooks. `Main` is spelled by the language.

**A custom awaitable counts, and is recognised by having a parameterless `GetAwaiter` rather than by being on a list.** Without that, a method returning somebody's own awaitable type and correctly named `…Async` would be reported for a suffix it has earned. `Task`, `Task<T>`, `ValueTask`, `ValueTask<T>` and `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` are named explicitly; an `async void` method counts as asynchronous, so an event handler named `…Async` is not reported for the return type it is obliged to have.

⚠ **No fix, and this refutes what the proposal asked for.** The repair is a rename, and a rename touches every call site. ADR-005 makes a Skala fix a minimal text-edit list against one file's original `SourceText`; an edit that renamed the declaration and nothing else would break the build on the tool's advice, which is the one thing a fix may never do. A rename is a workspace operation, not a text edit, and this rule is report-only until Skala has one.

**Local functions are not reported.** A local function's name is a detail of one body with no callers outside it, so the suffix carries no information there.

rules.title: The set or dictionary initializer repeats a key
rules.summary: Two entries of one set or dictionary initializer — or of one collection expression — carry the same constant key, so the collection ends up smaller than it was written or the construction throws.
rules.rationale: The three initializer forms fail in three different ways and none of them is what the author wrote. `{ { k, v }, { k, w } }` calls `Add` twice and `Dictionary<K, V>.Add` throws `ArgumentException` at construction — a field initializer doing that takes the type's constructor with it. `{ [k] = v, [k] = w }` assigns through the indexer, so the second write silently wins and `v` is evaluated and thrown away. `new HashSet<T> { a, a }` returns a set of one where two were written. In every case the object at the end of the initializer is not the object on the page, and the key is right there to compare.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Constant keys only.** `{ [a] = 1, [b] = 2 }` with two variables is not a finding even when `a` and `b` hold the same value at run time, because the analyzer has no way to know that and the shape is legitimate for a table built from names. An entry whose key is not a constant is skipped rather than blocking the entries around it. ⚠ **The comparer is not resolved — the rule declines whenever the constructor is given any argument at all.** Key equality belongs to the collection's comparer, not to the key type: `new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase) { ["a"] = 1, ["A"] = 2 }` throws where `"a" != "A"` ordinally, and a comparer can just as easily make two keys the rule thinks are equal distinct. Declining on *any* argument is deliberately broader than declining on a comparer argument: it costs a capacity-only initializer a true finding, and it means the rule never has to decide which parameter a comparer arrived through. ⚠ **The receiver must be one of `Dictionary`, `SortedDictionary`, `SortedList`, `ConcurrentDictionary`, `HashSet` or `SortedSet` as the semantic model resolves it.** A `List<T>` may repeat an element on purpose and a user collection's `Add` means whatever its author wrote, so neither is examined. ⚠ **The key type must be one whose default equality the analyzer can decide**: `string` (ordinal, which is what `EqualityComparer<string>.Default` does), `bool`, `char`, the integral types and any `enum`. `double`, `float`, `decimal`, a nullable key and every reference type other than `string` are declined. Two equal constants are still equal under a *sorted* collection's default `IComparer<T>`, which is why the sorted types are in the table; the reverse — two ordinally distinct strings a culture comparer would call equal — is not reported. Only the second and any later occurrence is reported, so three copies of one key give two findings and each points at a line that can be deleted. No fix: deleting the duplicate entry and correcting its key are the two available repairs, they produce different programs, and the analyzer has no way to tell which one was meant — and deleting the entry would discard a value expression that may have side effects. ⚠ **A collection expression is a different node kind, and a rule registered only on the initializer would quietly say nothing about it.** `new HashSet<T> { "a", "a" }` and `HashSet<T> s = ["a", "a"]` are one defect in two spellings and the second is the idiom now, so both are examined; a **spread** anywhere in a collection expression withdraws the whole finding rather than being stepped over, because a duplicate the spread supplies is not this rule's to report and one it hides is not this rule's to claim. ⚠ **`CA2244` overlaps the indexer form and only the indexer form**, and it is **not in the default .NET analysis set** — measured, not assumed: an ordinary `net10.0` SDK project with nothing configured reports `CA2200` on a control shape and says nothing about any of these three, so a repository that has not raised `AnalysisMode` sees no duplicate. `CA2244` also says nothing at all about the `Add` form, which is the one that throws at construction, or about a set that silently drops an element.

rules.title: The collection is passed to its own method as the other collection
rules.summary: A set, list or array is given to one of its own members as the second collection, where the answer is fixed, the call does nothing, or the collection is emptied or doubled.
rules.rationale: `set.UnionWith(set)` does nothing. `set.ExceptWith(set)` is `Clear()` written so that nobody reads it as `Clear()`. `set.SetEquals(set)` is `true` with a hash walk in front of it, `set.IsProperSubsetOf(set)` is `false`, and `list.AddRange(list)` doubles the list in place. Every entry in the table is a call whose result does not depend on what the collection holds, which is never why anybody writes one. The defect underneath is almost always a single identifier — the second collection was meant to be a different one — and that is also why there is no fix: naming the right collection is the repair, and the analyzer does not know which one it is.

examples.bad:
var stale = new HashSet<string>(known);
stale.ExceptWith(stale);
examples.good:
var stale = new HashSet<string>(known);
stale.ExceptWith(current);

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The two sides must be the same *storage*, which is a symbol comparison and not a text one.** `a.items` and `b.items` resolve to one field symbol through two different receivers, so the walk compares the receivers too and stops at the first symbol that differs; `items` and `this.items` are recognised as one storage because the member symbol already matched. ⚠ **Every symbol on the path must be a local, a parameter or a field.** A property is an accessor call and two reads of one property may hand back two different objects, so `Current.Items.UnionWith(Current.Items)` is not reported; an invocation or an indexer anywhere in the path is excluded for the same reason. ⚠ **`a.Equals(a)` is deliberately outside the table** even though it is the shape the upstream title suggests: asserting that a type's equality is reflexive is exactly what an equality test does, and this repository's own `SK2004` fixtures would be the first false positives. ⚠ **`Concat`, `Zip` and `Array.Copy` are outside it for the opposite reason**: `items.Concat(items)` is a legitimate way to say "twice", and `Array.Copy(buffer, 1, buffer, 0, n)` is how a shift is written. A degenerate result is the entry condition for the table, not an unusual-looking argument. The receiver is matched against concrete framework types — `HashSet<T>`, `SortedSet<T>`, `List<T>`, `System.Array` and the four `Enumerable` operators — never against `ISet<T>` or a user collection, where the member's meaning is its author's. A named argument or a `ref` argument anywhere in the call withdraws the finding, because the slot an argument occupies is then not the slot it is written in.

rules.title: The collection element is written twice with nothing reading it in between
rules.summary: One entry of a list, array or dictionary is assigned twice in a contiguous run of element writes, so the first value is computed and thrown away.
rules.rationale: A block of `map[…] = …;` statements is how a lookup table gets built by hand, and it is where one key gets written twice: the first value is computed, stored and discarded by a later statement, and nothing in the compiler notices because both writes are legal. Either a key is wrong or a line is redundant, and which of the two it is decides what the program was supposed to do — which is also why there is no fix.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Roslyn's `AnalyzeDataFlow` answers questions about variables, not about indexed elements**, so there is no dataflow behind this rule and it does not pretend to have any. It reports only a *contiguous run of element writes to one collection*: the moment a statement that is not such a write appears between the two, the finding is withdrawn. That is a fraction of the defect and it is the fraction that can be proved without a lattice — a loop, a branch, a method call or a `ref` escape between the writes all end the run. ⚠ **The run is additionally required to be opaque-free**: an invocation, an object creation, an `await`, a lambda, a nested assignment, a `++` or a `ref` argument anywhere in an intervening write ends it, and so does any mention of the collection itself on the right of one, because each is a place the first value could be read through an alias. ⚠ **"The keys are different" is a stronger claim than "the keys are not the same", and only two constants answer it.** Two variables may hold one value and a comparer may make two distinct-looking values one key, so an undecidable pair ends the run rather than being stepped over. Two keys are the same when they are equal constants — which every `IEqualityComparer<T>` agrees with, since equality is reflexive — or when they are one storage read twice. ⚠ **`ConcurrentDictionary` is not in the receiver table, deliberately**: the point of the type is that another thread may read between the two writes, so "nothing read it" is not something this analysis is entitled to say there. The receiver must be an array or one of `List<T>`, `Dictionary<K, V>`, `SortedDictionary<K, V>` or `SortedList<K, V>`; a user type's indexer setter may accumulate, log or dispatch, and two writes to one index there are two events rather than one lost value. Compound assignment (`c[k] += v`) is a read as well as a write and is never a candidate.

rules.title: The collection iterated here is provably empty
rules.summary: A local collection is created empty, is never referred to except as the subject of a foreach, and is then iterated — so the loop body cannot run.
rules.rationale: The population step was removed, or was never written. The loop reads as working code, the compiler has nothing to say about it, and every test over it passes, because a body that never runs never fails. The repair is the missing step, which is why there is no fix: deleting the loop would silence the rule and keep the defect.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **This is proved by exhaustion, not by dataflow.** Roslyn's `AnalyzeDataFlow` answers questions about variables and not about a collection's contents, so the rule asks a question it can answer instead: *every* reference to the local inside the member that declares it must be the subject of a `foreach`. A collection can only be filled through a member call, an assignment, or by being handed somewhere, and each of those is a reference that is not a `foreach` subject — so one reference of any other kind, including an argument, a receiver, an assignment target, a `ref` or a capture, withdraws the finding, and the analyzer never has to decide what that reference does. ⚠ **The scan runs over the whole enclosing member rather than forward from the declaration.** A lambda or local function declared before the local cannot capture it, and one declared after it holds a reference the scan sees, so the answer does not depend on ordering — which is what makes the exhaustion argument sound. ⚠ **Locals only.** A field or a property can be filled by any member of the type and by anything holding the instance, so "nothing adds to it" is not a claim available there. The initialiser must be an empty collection expression, an empty array, `Array.Empty<T>()`, `Enumerable.Empty<T>()`, or a parameterless construction of a known framework collection; **any constructor argument withdraws it**, because a capacity leaves the collection empty and a source collection does not, and declining both is cheaper than telling them apart. `foreach` over something that is not a plain name — an expression, a call, a member path — is not examined at all.

rules.title: Use an index-from-end expression
rules.summary: An element access whose index counts back from the collection's own `Count` or `Length` is an index-from-end expression.
rules.rationale: `items[items.Count - 1]` names the collection twice and subtracts, and the reader has to check that both names are the same collection before believing the expression means "the last one". `items[^1]` says it, names the receiver once, and cannot be written with the wrong collection on one side — the copy-paste defect this shape produces is exactly `a[b.Count - 1]`, which compiles and is wrong. The subtraction is also the arithmetic the compiler was going to emit anyway: `^1` lowers to `Count - 1`, so the rewrite costs nothing and removes the only place a person can get it wrong.

examples.bad:
var last = items[items.Count - 1];
var previous = buffer[buffer.Length - offset];
examples.good:
var last = items[^1];
var previous = buffer[^offset];

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **`^` is not available on everything that has a `Count`.** The language's implicit index support needs a countable type *and* an `int` indexer, and `IEnumerable<T>` has neither — so the rule reads the indexed type rather than the shape of the expression, and admits only an array, a `string`, a type with a real `System.Index` indexer (`Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`), or a type implementing `IList<T>`/`IReadOnlyList<T>`. ⚠ **`Dictionary<int, V>` is countable and has an `int` indexer, so `d[^1]` compiles** and means the entry keyed `Count - 1` — the same program, spelled as if it were the last element. The `IList<T>` restriction is what keeps that out, and it is the reason the rule is not simply "the type is countable". ⚠ The receiver of the element access and the receiver of `.Count`/`.Length` must be the same chain of plain names, so `a[b.Count - 1]` is never rewritten and nothing that could have a side effect is evaluated a different number of times. ⚠ **The subtrahend is admitted only as a positive integer literal or a plain `int`-typed name path.** `^0` is `Count`, which throws where `Count - 0` also throws but is a different sentence, and a negative constant reaches `Index`'s constructor, which throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` where the subtraction would have thrown `IndexOutOfRangeException`. ⚠ Silent below C# 8, silent inside an expression tree where the indexer pattern is not expressible, and silent where `System.Index` is not **accessible** — which is not the same question as whether it exists. `System.Memory` ships an *internal* `System.Index` for `netstandard2.0`, so a presence check alone reported sixteen findings on Skala's own `netstandard2.0` projects, every one of whose fixes failed to compile with `CS0518`. The gate is the compiler's own accessibility test. The rule is one shape with one floor, so the gate is per-rule.

rules.title: Use `nameof`
rules.summary: A name produced at run time — `typeof(T).Name`, an enum member's `ToString()` — or written as a literal in a position that is defined to hold an identifier.
rules.rationale: `nameof` is the only spelling of a name that a rename touches. `typeof(Widget).Name` and `Colour.Red.ToString()` compute at run time what the compiler already knows, and a literal `"count"` handed to `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`'s `paramName` is a name the compiler was never asked about at all — so it survives the rename that makes it wrong, and the first person to see the mistake is whoever reads the exception. This is disproportionately a generated-code problem: a model writes the string because the pre-C# 6 dialect it learned had nothing else to write.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **A string that happens to equal a member name is not a `nameof` candidate, and this rule never guesses.** Serialization keys, JSON property names, SQL column names, HTTP headers and `.editorconfig` keys are all literals that look exactly like identifiers and mean something a rename must *not* follow — rewriting one silently changes the wire format. There is no test that separates them from the intended ones, so the rule fires only in positions whose meaning is defined: a `paramName` parameter of the `ArgumentException` family, and a `PropertyChangedEventArgs`/`PropertyChangingEventArgs` constructor. ⚠ **`UseNameofExpressionForPartOfTheString` is deliberately not covered** for that reason; it is also the one of the three inspections that ships at `none`. ⚠ **`typeof(T).Name` is `nameof(T)` only for a non-generic named type spelled by its own name.** `typeof(List<int>).Name` is `` `List`1` `` and `nameof(List<int>)` is `List`; `typeof(int).Name` is `Int32` and `nameof(int)` does not compile; `typeof(T).Name` on a type parameter is the *argument's* name at run time; and a `using` alias makes `nameof` produce the alias where `Name` produces the type — so the last identifier of the written type must equal the symbol's own name. Arrays, nullable spellings and `dynamic` are all refused. ⚠ **An enum member's `ToString()` is its name only when the value is unique.** `enum E { A = 1, B = 1 }` makes `E.B.ToString()` return `"A"`, so the rule reads every field of the enum and declines a shared value. ⚠ `SK2017` reports the `paramName` literal that names *no* parameter and this rule reports the one that does, so the two never both fire. Every shape is silent inside an expression tree and below C# 6, and the four shapes share that one floor, so the gate is per-rule.

rules.title: Use the string literal form that needs no escapes
rules.summary: An escaped or verbatim literal a raw string would write without escapes, a raw string whose delimiter is longer than it needs to be, or an escape sequence that is simply a character.
rules.rationale: Escape-dense literals — Windows paths, embedded JSON, regexes — are where a stray backslash changes the meaning of the string and nothing says so. `"\\d+\\.\\d+"` and `"{\"id\":1}"` have to be decoded by the reader before they can be checked against whatever they are supposed to match, and the decoding is where the mistake gets made. A raw string removes the escaping entirely, and the shortest correct delimiter is the one that says the content has no quotes to worry about.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The delimiter is the rule and getting it wrong emits code that does not compile.** A single-line raw string's fence is the longest run of quotes in the content plus one, never fewer than three, and its content may not begin or end with a quote at all. Rather than trusting that arithmetic, every replacement this rule proposes is **re-parsed as an expression and its value compared against the original's** before the finding is reported — a wrong fence cannot become a diagnostic, let alone a fix. ⚠ **Only single-line forms are touched.** A value containing a newline, a tab, or any other control character has no single-line raw spelling, and a multi-line raw string carries indentation rules that make the rewrite a formatting decision rather than a mechanical one. ⚠ **Version-gated per shape, not per rule.** The three raw-string shapes are silent below C# 11; simplifying an escape sequence to the character it denotes has no floor at all, and a single rule-level floor would have silenced it on every older project. ⚠ `\x` is variable-length and greedy — `"\x41B"` is one escape denoting U+041B, not `\x41` followed by `B` — so the scan consumes it the way the lexer does and then declines it, because the character is outside the printable ASCII range the shape admits. `\\`, `\"`, `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\0` and `\U` are never simplified. ⚠ A literal inside an interpolation hole is left alone: `SK1063` has its own opinion about those, and two rules rewriting one span is one of them being wrong. ⚠ **`UseVerbatimString` is not covered** — this rule goes to the raw form and never produces a verbatim one, and crediting an inspection whose output it does not reproduce would overstate the parity.

rules.title: Use the interpolation form that says what it means
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ The export sets `resharper_use_string_interpolation_when_possible_highlighting` to `hint` and this rule defaults to `suggestion`. ReSharper's inspection covers the whole `string.Format` surface, including the argument shapes whose rewrite is not sound, so a low severity is how it stays usable; this rule declines those shapes by analysis instead and can afford to be seen. Reading the ReSharper key would lower it. docs/plan/16 § Q5.
rules.summary: A `string.Format` whose holes are numbered, a `ToString()` inside an interpolation hole, or a string literal sitting in a hole instead of in the text.
rules.rationale: `string.Format("{0} of {1}", done, total)` makes the reader carry two numbers across a comma to find out what goes where, and the compiler will not tell them when the arguments are swapped. The interpolated form puts the value where it is printed. The two smaller shapes are the same argument applied to interpolation itself: `$"{count.ToString()}"` renders through a string nobody keeps, and `$"a{"b"}c"` is a hole holding something that was never a variable.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **`SK2016` reports the one place interpolation must not be used**, and this rule must not create that finding: a `string.Format` whose result is handed to a `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging` `message` parameter is left alone, because rewriting it would eagerly render the message the logger was going to render lazily. ⚠ **Overload resolution is the trap that makes the rewrite unsound where it bites.** An interpolated string converts to `string`, to `FormattableString` and to `IFormattable`, so a call site with a `FormattableString` overload beside the `string` one — EF Core's `FromSql` family is the well-known case — can bind somewhere else after the rewrite, and there the difference is whether the SQL is parameterised. The rule reads the member group at the call site and declines if any candidate takes `FormattableString` or `IFormattable` in that position. ⚠ **The placeholders must be `{0}`…`{n-1}`, each used exactly once and in ascending order.** A repeated index would evaluate its argument twice; an out-of-order one would evaluate the arguments in a different order; a gap means an argument is unused. Every argument must be a chain of plain names, so nothing with a comma or a colon in it lands inside a hole, where both are grammar. The `IFormatProvider` overloads are refused outright — the culture is the point of them — as are a non-literal or verbatim format string and an explicitly passed `object[]`. ⚠ **`x.ToString()` inside a hole is removable only for a value type.** On a reference type `null.ToString()` throws where `$"{null}"` renders empty, which is not a modernization but a behaviour change; `Nullable<T>` is admitted because both spellings render the empty string. A hole carrying a format clause is left alone. ⚠ **Not covered, deliberately:** `NestedStringInterpolation`, `PassStringInterpolation`, and `UseFormatSpecifierInFormatString` — the last because `x.ToString("N2")` and `$"{x:N2}"` agree only where the instance method delegates to `IFormattable`, which the BCL numeric types do and a user type need not.

rules.title: Use `>>>`
rules.summary: A cast to the unsigned type, a right shift, and a cast back is the unsigned right shift operator.
rules.rationale: `(int)((uint)x >> n)` is three operations spelling one, and two of the three are the casts that sign extension bugs come out of — a reader has to check that the widths match before believing the round trip is lossless, and the compiler will not check it for them. `x >>> n` is the operation, at the operand's own width, with nothing to get wrong.

examples.bad: var high = (int)((uint)hash >> 16);
examples.good: var high = hash >>> 16;

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The equivalence holds only where the two types are the same width, and `>>` does not preserve width below 32 bits.** `(short)((ushort)x >> n)` looks identical and is a different program: `ushort` promotes to `int` before the shift, so the value shifted is zero-extended, while `x >>> n` on a `short` promotes the *signed* value first. For `x = -1` and `n = 4` the first gives 4095 and the second gives -1. Only `int`/`uint` and `long`/`ulong` are admitted, where `>>` is defined at the declared width; `byte`, `sbyte`, `short`, `ushort` and the native integer types are refused. The operand's own static type must be the signed one, so `(int)(u >> n)` on an already-unsigned `u` is not this shape. ⚠ **A `checked` context breaks the equivalence in both casts.** `(uint)x` throws for a negative `x` and `(int)u` throws for a `u` above `int.MaxValue`, where `>>>` never throws — so the rule is silent inside `checked` and silent entirely when the compilation sets `CheckForOverflowUnderflow`. ⚠ **`>>>` binds far more loosely than a cast**, so `(int)((uint)x >> n) + 1` rewritten bare would become `x >>> (n + 1)`. Rather than inventing parentheses the author did not write, the rule declines every position where the surrounding expression could rebind and fires only where a shift may stand unparenthesised. One shape with one floor, so the gate is per-rule.

rules.title: Deconstruct the tuple instead of reading it element by element
rules.summary: Consecutive `var` declarations read every element of one tuple in order, which is a deconstruction written out longhand.
rules.rationale: Deconstruction arrived with tuples in C# 7 and is the form the language was given the tuple for; a model writes the `Item1`/`Item2` reads because most of its training data is older than both. The longhand form also loses the one thing the tuple was carrying — that the pieces belong together — and `var a = t.Item1;` names the variable twice while naming what it holds not at all.

examples.good:
var pair = Split(text);
var (key, value) = pair;

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Deconstruction evaluates the receiver once and the longhand form evaluates it once per element, so the receiver has to be something re-reading cannot observe.** The rule requires it to be a single identifier naming a *local or a parameter*: reading one N times and reading it once are then the same program by construction, which is a stronger claim than the usual "no invocation in the path" and is the reason no property or field receiver is matched. ⚠ **A partial deconstruction is not this rule.** Every element of the tuple must be read, exactly once, in positional order, by consecutive single-declarator statements — `var a = t.Item1;` on its own is one variable with a name, not a deconstruction missing three quarters of itself. ⚠ **Every declaration must be `var`.** `var (a, b) = t;` gives each variable the element's type; a written type on one of the longhand declarations means the author asked for a different type, and reproducing that needs the typed deconstruction form the fix does not emit. ⚠ Only real tuple types — `System.ValueTuple` and its language syntax — are matched. `System.Tuple<T1, T2>` deconstructs only through the `System.TupleExtensions` extension methods, so the rewrite would depend on a `using` the file may not have. ⚠ Declarations carrying modifiers, attributes, `const`, `using`, `await` or `ref` are excluded, as is any run whose span holds a comment or a preprocessor directive, because the fix deletes those lines.
rules.resharperNote: ⚠ The export sets `resharper_use_deconstruction_highlighting = hint` and this rule defaults to `suggestion`. Reading the ReSharper key therefore *lowers* the rule below its default, and a repository importing an untouched ReSharper export will see it dimmed. The default is deliberate: JetBrains rates it a hint because it is a style nicety in an IDE that offers the rewrite under a keystroke, and Skala's audience is an agent writing the longhand form into a file nobody is going to press a keystroke in. `SwapViaDeconstruction`, `UsePositionalDeconstructionPattern` and `MoveToExistingPositionalDeconstructionPattern` are three further inspections in the same family and none of them is covered here.

rules.title: Copy the record with a `with` expression
rules.summary: A record is copied by calling its own constructor back with its own members, which is what `with` is for.
rules.rationale: A copy that respells every member is a copy that silently drops the next member added to the type: the constructor call still compiles, still passes the new parameter *something*, and nobody looking at the copy site can see that a field stopped travelling. `with` is the shape that cannot go stale, because the members it does not name are the ones it copies.

examples.bad:
public Settings WithRetries(Settings settings, int retries) =>
    new Settings(settings.Host, settings.Port, retries);
examples.good:
public Settings WithRetries(Settings settings, int retries) =>
    settings with { Retries = retries };

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **`with` invokes the record's copy constructor, which copies *every* field — including the ones the hand-written call deliberately dropped — so the rule is only sound where the record has no state beyond its positional parameters, and that is proved rather than assumed.** The record must be `sealed` (or a `record struct`), must derive from no other record, must declare no instance field and no instance event, and every one of its positional properties must be the property that parameter itself declared — asked by comparing the two symbols' declaring syntax, since a positional property and its parameter are the same piece of source. A hand-written accessor in the record body would be called by `settings.Host` and *not* called by the copy constructor, which moves the backing field across without asking. ⚠ `IsImplicitlyDeclared` is the obvious test for that and is the wrong one: it is **false** for a positional record property, because the parameter is where the property is written down, and reading it as true silently disables the rule everywhere. It also means only records declared in source are matched, because a record from metadata has no declaring syntax to compare and nothing else in the symbol separates the two. A record deriving from another carries state `GetMembers` does not return, and an unsealed one is worse — `settings with { … }` calls the virtual clone and returns the runtime type, where `new Settings(…)` returns exactly `Settings`. ⚠ **At least one argument must be replaced.** A call that carries every member across unchanged would rewrite to `settings with { }`, which is `SK0230`'s finding and not this one, so the two never report the same code. ⚠ The receiver must be a single identifier naming a local or a parameter of exactly the record's type, and must not be assigned anywhere in the enclosing member: `with` evaluates the receiver once and clones before any initializer runs, so an argument that reassigns the receiver would make the two forms read different objects. Arguments must all be positional, with no `ref`, `out`, `in` or named argument. ⚠ The nested case `x with { A = x.A with { B = … } }` is not covered, and neither are the struct, tuple and anonymous-object inspections of the same ReSharper family. ⚠ The creation must sit where a `with` expression does not need parentheses — a declaration, a `return`, an expression body, an argument, a simple assignment or an initializer element — because `with` binds looser than member access.

rules.title: The spread of a freshly created array is its elements
rules.summary: An array is created inside a collection expression only so that a spread element can take it apart again.
rules.rationale: `SK1001` introduces collection expressions; this is the cleanup that follows one. An array built at the point of a spread lives for the length of one expression and exists only to be enumerated back into the collection that is being built beside it — the allocation, the copy and the `..` are all ceremony around a list of elements that could simply have been written there. A modernization rule without its cleanup family produces churn.

examples.bad: int[] codes = [.. new[] { 200, 204 }, fallback];
examples.good: int[] codes = [200, 204, fallback];

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The array's element type and the outer collection's element type must be the same symbol, and that is not fussiness about a widening nobody would notice.** Before the rewrite each element is converted twice — to the array's element type, and from there to the outer collection's; after it, once. Two conversions in sequence are not the same as the one that would replace them: `new long[] { anInt }` spread into a `double[]` goes `int → long → double` and would go `int → double`, and where a user-defined conversion is on either leg the single step does not exist at all, because C# never chains two of them — so the fix would not even compile. Requiring the two element types to be equal makes both sides one conversion and removes the question. Where the outer collection's element type cannot be determined — a type implementing `IEnumerable<T>` twice, a builder-attributed target — the rule declines. ⚠ Only an array creation carrying a written initializer is matched: `new T[] { … }` and `new[] { … }`, single-dimension, at least one element, no `{ k, v }` pair among them. A nested collection expression as the spread operand has no type of its own to compare against, and a spread of anything that was not created on the spot is a spread of something the program can still see. ⚠ An **empty** creation is deliberately not matched. `[.. new T[0], a]` is `[a]`, which deletes a separator as well as an element; the empty-collection concept is `SK1073`'s and `CA1825`'s. ⚠ The elements are carried across as source text rather than rebuilt from syntax, so a comment or an alignment between them survives; the text on either side of them, which the fix deletes, is checked for a comment or a directive first. ⚠ Four further inspections in this ReSharper family are not covered: `AppendToCollectionExpression`, the two `UseArrayCreationExpression` forms and `RedundantArrayCreationExpression` outside a spread.

rules.title: Use the framework's cached instance
rules.summary: A stateless framework value is constructed where the framework already holds one: `new EventArgs()` is `EventArgs.Empty`.
rules.rationale: `new EventArgs()` allocates an object with no state, on an event that may be raised in a loop, where `EventArgs.Empty` is already there. The three struct cases cost nothing at run time and are a readability finding instead: `Guid.Empty`, `TimeSpan.Zero` and `CancellationToken.None` say what the value *is*, where `new Guid()` says only how it was made. Every one of them is a name a model writes the long way round because the long way round is what most of its training data does.

examples.bad:
Changed?.Invoke(this, new EventArgs());
if (id == new Guid()) { }
examples.good:
Changed?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty);
if (id == Guid.Empty) { }

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **The table is four entries long and every one of them carries its own proof, because "there is a cached instance" is not a property that generalizes.** `EventArgs` has no instance state and no member that could tell one instance from another, so `EventArgs.Empty` and a fresh one differ only by reference identity. `Guid.Empty`, `TimeSpan.Zero` and `CancellationToken.None` are the default value of a struct, where identity is not observable at all. The member is looked up on the resolved type and required to be a static field or property of that same type before anything is reported — a table that assumed the member exists would report a fix that does not compile the day a framework drops one. ⚠ **The zero-length-array half of this concept is deliberately absent: `new T[0]` is `CA1825`, which ships in the SDK, and ADR-008 hosts rather than rebuilds.** ⚠ **A parameter's default value is the trap.** `void M(TimeSpan t = new TimeSpan())` compiles and `= TimeSpan.Zero` does not, because a default must be a compile-time constant and a static readonly field is not one; the same holds for an attribute argument and a constant pattern, and all of them are excluded by position. ⚠ The type must be the framework's: it is resolved by metadata name and required to come from a referenced assembly, so a source type of the same name is never matched. Only a creation with no arguments and no initializer, and only `default(T)` written with its type — a bare `default` takes its type from a context this rule does not re-derive. A target-typed `new()` is not matched either, because there is no written type to build the replacement from; the fix reproduces the type exactly as the file spells it, so an alias or a `using`-shortened name stays spelled that way and no `using` is required that the file does not have. ⚠ `EventArgs.Empty` is a singleton, so code comparing event arguments by reference would see a change — the residual false positive, and the reason the entry is worth stating rather than assuming.

rules.title: The Serilog message template has a different number of holes than the call supplies values
rules.summary: A Serilog logging call's constant message template declares a number of holes that is not the number of values the call passes.
rules.rationale: The rendered event is wrong in both directions and neither direction throws. A hole with no value is emitted as the literal text `{OrderId}`, so the field a dashboard queries is never populated and the message reads as a bug report about itself; a value with no hole is attached under a fabricated positional key nobody queries, so the data is present, unfindable and paid for. ⚠ **The rule is deliberately Serilog-only.** `CA2017` already covers `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging` — measured against `LoggerExtensions`, `ILogger.BeginScope` and `LoggerMessage.Define`, handling `{{` escapes, `{X,10:N2}` alignment and declining a non-implicit `params` array — and unlike `CA2241`, `CA2253` and `CA2254` it is **on by default**, with no `AnalysisMode` required. ADR-008 hosts `CA*` rather than rebuilding them, so what Skala implements is the half with no host at all. Serilog is where the concept is unowned, and it is also where the shape is commonest, because Serilog's own API encourages templates far richer than `ILogger`'s.

examples.bad: logger.Information("Loaded {Count} of {Total}", count);
examples.good: logger.Information("Loaded {Count} of {Total}", count, total);

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **`resharperId` is deliberately null.** ReSharper dumps one issue type for this whole family, `StructuredMessageTemplateProblem`, and `Testing/parity-analysis/catalogued.json` already credits it to `SK2016`. Moving another rule's credit is a decision about a hand-written map rather than a fact about this rule, and the map is the artefact doc 17 § "Two corrections" was written about. The concept is recorded against issue #20 in `ledger-resharper.json` instead. ⚠ **Arity is counted in holes, not in distinct names.** `"{X} then {X}"` with two arguments is correct — Serilog binds values to holes in order — and reporting it here would be a false positive on exactly the shape `SK2071` exists to describe properly. ⚠ **A positional template withdraws the analysis entirely.** `"{0} {1}"` is Serilog's `string.Format` mode, where arity is max-index-plus-one rather than a count, and a template mixing indices with names has semantics no rule should guess at; `CA2253` is the rule that says not to write one. ⚠ **A `params` array the call did not synthesise withdraws the count**: `logger.Information(template, args)` passes an array whose length is not visible here, and counting the array itself as one value would report every such call as a mismatch. Roslyn marks the array it synthesises for a genuine `params` expansion as implicit, which is the only signal that separates the two. ⚠ **The values are counted by parameter ordinal**, never by filtering out arguments whose type does not look like a value: a reduced extension-method invocation carries its own `this ILogger` receiver as `Arguments[0]` with a real parameter symbol, and a type-name filter counts the logger as a supplied value and reports every correct call as one argument too many. Everything that is not a value — the receiver, the `Exception`, the `LogEventLevel` — precedes the template in every one of these signatures, so "after the template" is a definition rather than a heuristic. A non-constant template is not analysed, because there is no template to count; `CA2254` is the rule for that. Binding is by containing type (`Serilog.ILogger`, `Serilog.Log`) and by the parameter Serilog names `messageTemplate`, never by method name, so a domain method called `Information` is not a logging call. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: The structured log template names the same property twice
rules.summary: A logging call's constant message template uses one property name for more than one hole, so the structured event cannot carry both values.
rules.rationale: The rendered line looks right, which is what makes this one survive review. The structured event is the part that is wrong: one key cannot hold two values, so a sink keeps one of them and the other is gone, and which one survives is the sink's business rather than the author's. The field a dashboard filters on is then silently either the first value or the last. ⚠ **Nothing hosts this, for any logging framework.** `CA2017` counts *holes* against arguments, so `logger.LogInformation("{X} then {X}", a, b)` is arity-correct and it stays silent — measured in a probe project, at default analysis level and at `AnalysisMode=All`, rather than read from documentation. That is why this rule covers `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging` as well as Serilog, where `SK2070` deliberately does not: the concept has no host anywhere, so ADR-008 has nothing to defer to. There is no fix, because the second property's name is the thing the author has to choose and no edit can choose it.

examples.bad: logger.LogInformation("Moved {Path} to {Path}", from, to);
examples.good: logger.LogInformation("Moved {From} to {To}", from, to);

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **`{@Order}` and `{Order}` are the same property and are reported.** Serilog's `@` (destructure) and `$` (stringify) sigils select how a value is captured, not what it is called; a parser that keeps the sigil sees two names where the logger sees one and misses the duplicate this rule exists to find. ⚠ **Comparison is ordinal, so `{Count}` and `{count}` are two properties and neither is reported.** They are two properties to every sink there is, so no value is lost and calling them a duplicate would be an opinion about naming dressed as a defect. ⚠ **The finding is reported on the whole template argument rather than on the repeated name.** A hole's offset is known within the template's *value*, and the value and the source spelling diverge at the first escape sequence — one `\n` earlier in the literal and a span computed from the value points one character short. A slightly coarse span that is always right beats a precise one that is quietly wrong inside a baseline fingerprint. ⚠ **One finding per repeated name, not one per extra occurrence**: a name written three times is one decision, and reporting it twice would report the same decision as many times as it was made. `{{` and `}}` are escapes and are not holes. A positional template (`"{0} {0}"`) withdraws the analysis, because indices are `string.Format` semantics rather than property names; `CA2253` is the rule that says not to write one. A non-constant template is not analysed. Binding is by containing type (`Serilog.ILogger`, `Serilog.Log`, `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LoggerExtensions`) and by the parameter each spells `messageTemplate`, `message` or `messageFormat`, never by method name, so a domain method called `Information` is not a logging call. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: The literal contains an unescaped invisible character
rules.summary: A string or character literal holds a zero-width, bidirectional or control character written as itself rather than as an escape sequence.
rules.rationale: A zero-width space, a non-breaking space or a right-to-left override pasted into a literal is invisible in the editor, in the diff and in the review, and it changes what the program does — a key that never matches, a header that never parses, a path that is not the path anybody read. The escape sequence is the same value written so a person can see it, which is why the fix is mechanical and safe. ⚠ **Two classes of character, one severity, and that is a decision rather than an oversight.** A right-to-left override is the "Trojan Source" class — source that reads as one program and compiles as another — and a stray non-breaking space is a typo. The message says which one it found; the severity does not, because splitting them would spend a second permanent id (ADR-012) to encode a ranking, and a repository that wants the harder line writes `dotnet_diagnostic.SK2072.severity = error` without needing one.

examples.bad: public const string Tenant = "tenant\u200Bid";   // written with the character itself
examples.good: public const string Tenant = "tenant\\u200Bid";  // written as an escape

rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Reported only where an escape is expressible.** A verbatim (`@"…"`) or raw (`"""…"""`) literal has no escape sequences at all — that is what those literals are for — and a UTF-8 literal is a separate token kind for the same reason, so all three are silent. ⚠ **That is a real hole rather than a tidy boundary**: a bidirectional override inside a raw string literal is exactly as dangerous and is not reported, and the honest form of that is to say so rather than to emit a finding with no repair. ⚠ **The scan reads the token's source spelling, never its value**, which is what makes an already-escaped character silent: in the raw text it is six ASCII characters. Reading the value would report the repair as the problem and the rule would never go quiet. ⚠ **Confusable-*width* spaces are deliberately absent from the set** — U+2000 to U+200A and U+3000 — because a thin space in typography and an ideographic space in Japanese text are visible, intentional and correct, and reporting them would make the rule an opinion about typesetting. U+00A0 and U+202F stay, because they are indistinguishable from an ordinary space rather than merely narrower than one. Comments and identifiers are not literals and are not scanned; a soft hyphen in an identifier is a naming question that `IDE1006` is nearer to. `\n` and `\r` are absent from the control set because the language will not carry them: a raw newline in a regular string literal does not compile. The fix always writes `\uXXXX` and never `\xNN`, because `\x` is variable length and consumes greedily — `\x9` followed by `G` is a different character in one case and a compile error in another. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: The caught exception is not passed to the logger's exception parameter
rules.summary: An error-level logging call inside a catch clause does not give the logger the exception the clause caught, although the overload that takes one exists.
rules.rationale: Every one of these APIs takes the exception in its own parameter, and that parameter is what a sink treats as an exception: it is where the stack trace, the inner chain and the type end up as structure rather than as a sentence in a message. Left empty, the entry says something went wrong and carries nothing anybody can act on, which is the whole reason the line was written. ⚠ **This is `SK7xxx` on the issue and `SK2xxx` here.** An entry that cannot be diagnosed from is a defect in the program's observable behaviour rather than a maintenance cost, and the same argument that puts `SK2014` — a `catch` that swallows without logging or rethrow — in the correctness band puts this next to it.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **Error and critical levels only** (`LogError`, `LogCritical`, `Error`, `Fatal`). An information- or debug-level line inside a `catch` is very often deliberate — an expected exception, handled, noted in passing — and reporting those is how a rule about logging becomes noise about control flow. ⚠ **Nothing is reported unless the repair exists**: the analysis looks up an overload with an `exception` parameter on the logging type first, so a logger that has none has no defect this rule can name and the fix cannot assume an overload into being. ⚠ **Only the `Log*(template, values…)` shape is reported, and that is a correctness constraint rather than caution.** `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging` orders its event-id overload `(EventId, Exception, string)`, so an exception prepended in front of an event id does not bind — `skala fix` would have broken the build on the tool's own advice. A call that writes anything before the template is declined outright rather than reported with a fix that cannot be applied. ⚠ **A call that already passes the exception as a *template argument* still fires**, because the `exception` parameter is still empty and a sink still gets a string where it expected an exception; the fix attaches the exception and does **not** also delete the now-redundant hole, because removing text from inside a literal needs a value-to-source offset map that escape sequences break, and a fix that is right except after a `\n` is worse than one that leaves a tidy-up for the author. A `catch` with no declared variable (`catch { }`, `catch (IOException)`) has no exception to pass and is silent. The nearest enclosing `catch` is the one used, and the walk stops at the member declaration rather than at the first `try`, so a lambda or local function written inside a `catch` — which really does close over the variable — is still reported. Binding is by containing type (`Serilog.ILogger`, `Serilog.Log`, `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LoggerExtensions`), never by method name. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: The logger is declared for a different type than the one that declares it
rules.summary: A type declares an ILogger<T> field, property or constructor parameter whose T is neither itself nor one of its base types.
rules.rationale: The type argument is the log *category*. A class holding an `ILogger<Other>` files every message it ever writes under another class's name, so a filter that selects this class misses them and a filter that selects the other one collects messages it never sent. Nothing fails, nothing is slow, and every log query about either class is quietly wrong — which is worse than noise, because noise is visible. The fix is mechanical: the category the declaration meant is the type the declaration is in. ⚠ **This is the objective quarter of issue #237, and the other three members are declined on purpose.** `S6669` (what the field is *named*) and `S1312` (whether it is `private static readonly`) are naming and declaration conventions, which are the most opinionated thing a linter can hold and a repository's to settle rather than a defect anybody can be shown. `S3416`'s `LogManager.GetLogger(typeof(Other))` shape is covered here only where the category is a declared `ILogger<T>`; Serilog's `Log.ForContext<T>()` is deliberately out, because choosing a context other than the enclosing type is a normal and intended use of that method rather than a mistake.
rules.falsePositives: ⚠ **A base type of the declaring type is accepted.** A hierarchy that files its whole family under the base class's category is a deliberate grouping, and the type argument still names something whose declaration the reader can find. Only an unrelated type is reported. ⚠ **Fields, properties and constructor parameters only** — the places a type *keeps* a logger. A `typeof(ILogger<Other>)`, a local in a composition root, a factory's return type and a method parameter that forwards one all name another class's logger on purpose, and reporting them would turn a rule about one type's own category into a rule against dependency injection. ⚠ **A type parameter is never reported**: `ILogger<T>` inside a generic helper is a category decided at the use site, not a wrong one, and there is no name a fix could write in its place. Comparison is on original definitions, so `Repository<T>` holding an `ILogger<Repository<T>>` is correct and the fix writes the type parameter list back. ⚠ **`defaultSeverity` is `suggestion` rather than `none`, and the measured count that would have argued for `none` does not exist**: Skala's own tree contains no `ILogger<T>` declaration at all — the shape is absent, verified by grep and by a probe file that made the rule fire once inserted — so a Skala count cannot show the rule is noisy. What settles it is that the finding is not a preference: `SK7010` and `SK7101` ship at `none` because a reader may reasonably disagree with them, and nobody reasonably wants their messages filed under another class's name. Generated code is excluded.

rules.title: An exception is thrown out of an `async void` body
rules.summary: A `throw` inside an `async void` method or local function, where nothing between it and the body's edge can catch it.
rules.rationale: An `async void` method has nowhere to put an exception. There is no task to fault, so the compiler-generated builder hands it to whatever `SynchronizationContext` was captured — and where there is none, which is every console application and every thread-pool callback, that is an unhandled exception on a pool thread and the process ends. The caller's `try`/`catch` never sees it, because the caller returned at the first `await`. A `catch` that logs and then rethrows is therefore strictly worse than no handler at all: it turns a recorded failure into a terminated process.
